1.	Were any representations made to the government or to any member thereof, or to any official of the Finance Department, by the Canadian Bankers Association, or any private individual, during the past two years, in the nature of a warning as to the instability of the Farmers''Bank of Canada?
2.	If so, what action was taken by the government for the protection of the shareholders and depositors of the said bank?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: 1 and 2. So far as the records of the Department of Finance show no such representations were made during the time referred to. The transactions in which the Farmers' Bank, through its General Manager, became implicated in December, 1909, with the First National Bank of Syracuse, New York, and the alleged obligation of the Farmers' Bank on a deposit receipt for $150,000 in such connection, were brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance, but beyond suggesting the irregularity and impropriety of these transactions there was nothing in the correspondence received to indicate that the Farmers' Bank, by these transactions, came into a position of ' instability.' The whole matter was fully discussed in the Toronto press at the time and the shareholders and depositors had ample notice of the character of these transactions. Ultimately, the Department of Finance was credibly advised that there was no obligation of the Farmers' Bank in the above connection, and that the alleged deposit receipt was returned to the bank. The correspondence in this connection will form part of a return now ordered by the House. The only evidence, during the time in question, from which the ' instability ' of the bank might be inferred and which came directly to the attention of the Finance Department, was in the form of broker's lists of market valuations. . In these lists Farmers' Bank stock was quoted as equal to half its paid up value and lesser sums. These indications of value were circulated by brokers for the information of the public including shareholders and depositors in the bank. Upon information of this character no action which the government could reasonably and legally take would improve the position of the shareholders.

1.	What is being done by the government to prevent the assets of the defunct Farmers' Bank from being sacrificed or eaten up in useless and unnecessary legal expenses?
2.	What steps are being taken by the government to ascertain the value of the Keeley mine property, an asset of the defunct Farmers' Bank, and whatever value there is in it being preserved for the benefit of the depositors and shareholders?

speechtext: Very good; I have not heard my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) for some little time.

There is no objection at all to bringing down the returns in answer to these two motions. With regard to the work of dredging the Rivier des Prairies, I may say that when the matter was first brought to my attention, it was urged that the channel would give accommodation for motor or pleasure boats. I was not greatly impressed with the argument in that respect, but later on my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Wilson), had a delegation wait upon me and presented petitions, and made very strong representations that the improvement of the Riviere des Prairies would be of great advantage to the farmers, in enabling them to get their produce to market by water at a much cheaper rate than by rail. On the invitation of the hon. member for Laval, (Mr. Wilson), I had the pleasure of visiting the Riviere des Prairies last summer, and I would say to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that I was greatly impressed with the advantages which w^ould accrue from opening up and improving the waterway between

the St. Lawrence river and the Lake of Two Mountains. I concluded, however, that the work from the lower end of the Riviere des Prairies was more important, or rather that the improvement there was more urgently required than further up. That is where the work has been done during the past season. I have asked from parliament a further amount to continue this work and the intention is, as the money is provided, to continue the work up to the Lake of Two Mountains. However, for the present, I think the work on the lower part of the river is the most important, because it will afford better means of communication between that very beautiful and very rich section of the country, and the city of Montreal, than if we had begun tire work further up in the first instance. But later on, as the moneys are provided I expect to continue the work right up to the Lake of Two Mountains.
Do I understand the minister to consent to the adoption of these two motions ?
Yes, to each of the two separately.

I would like to say that years before my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson), came to this House, and when he was still in the lower latitudes of provincial politics, I asked the chief of the Public" Works department to carry out this work for the reasons which have been indicated now by my hon. friend from Laval. I repeatedlv invited the Minister of Public Works to visit the locality, but I have never found him disposed to accept my hospitality. However, the advantages of, and need for, this work were pointed out by me more than 12 years ago.

I quite agree to a certain extent with the remarks of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), except on one point. When this appropriation was asked last year for the dredging of the river, it was my intention and as a matter of fact, I communicated it to the" Minister of Public Works, that the work should be started at both ends of the river. But, when we came to commence the work, we found we could not find a suitable dredge for operations on the upper part of the river, and it was thought better to start from the main channel of the St. Lawrence, so that the navigation which formerly existed between St. Vincent de Paul and the St. Lawrence river, might be restored. I understand from the minister, that there is no objection (if the report of the engineer which is already in the department, endorses it), that the work will be completed next year if possible.

May I ask my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Wilson), as he seems to 69i
have taken an interest in the matter, if the work on the upper part of the river is going to be carried out next year ?

I understand that depends on the report of the engineer. My information is, that there was not a suitable dredge to start the work at the Lake of Two Mountains, and as a matter of fact, the only dredge adapted for the work, is known as an orange peel dredge-
This looks like a lemon.
That dredge can work in five or six or eight feet of water, and the dredges which belong to the department of Public Works draw too much water to go down by the rapids.

He said: For some time past I have been endeavouring to get better facilities than now exist for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in the province of Nova Scotia. As far back as 1905, when I first entered this House, I had some negotiations with the then Minister of Justice, now Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, and the then judge of the Admiralty Court, and my proposition at that time was to form of the island of Cape Breton, or its four counties, into a separate admiralty district. However, something happened at that time to prevent that proposition from being put into operation. The then Minister of Justice and the late judge of the Admiralty Court both agreed that it was necessary to improve the situation in the province of Neva Scotia, and to give us better facilities for the administration of the business of that court than we then had. In the year 1908 a resolution was introduced by the present Minister of Justice proposing, by a Bill to be brought into the House, to give us the kind of facilities we desired. The Bill reached only its first reading on the 12th of March, 1908, and for some reason or other was dropped, and nothing much has been said about it since. Now, in the province of Nova Scotia, as well as in the other provinces of the Dominion, there is a great deal of work for this oourt to do.. My complaint is not that the law and the practice are not properly administered by the court now dealing with it. We have had, for many years, a very capable gentleman at the head of that court, at one time Minister of Justice of this Dominion and afterwards chief justice of our own province. He is not now, however, actively

engaged in the administration of that court, but we have in his place one of the fudges of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, who is well able' to discharge the duties devolving upon him. What I am complaining of is not the law, or the practice of the court, but the difficulties in the way of starting proceedings in the court. It will be observed, on looking at the Admiralty Act of this House, being chapter 141 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, that there is only one place in each province where a writ of the Admiralty Court can be issued-for the province of Ontario, in the city of Toronto; for the province of Quebec, in the city of Quebec; for the province of Nova Scotia, in the city of Halifax; for the province of New Brunswick, in the city of St. John; for the province of Prince Edward Island, in the city of Charlottetown. It is well known that in Nova Scotia the admiralty business extends to every part of the province. In the port from which I come there entered last year over 1,000 large steamers, only a few ships in number below the num-[DOT] ber that entered the grjat national port of Montreal. Out of this business there arise a great many complications, requiring the speedy exercise of the jurisdiction of the A.dmiralty Court, and it is 'exceedingly awkward to be obliged to go to Halifax, a distance of some 300 miles, before we can issue a writ. The proceedings against a ship are different from those against a person. A writ against a ship can only be issued while the ship is within the bounds of the province, and often claims are lost to seamen, salvers and towboats because the ship against which the claims lie gets out of the jurisdiction before it is possible to gat the papers from Halifax to proceed against her. It is not necessary to argue that it is not sufficient to have good laws, but that it is equally necessary to have those laws executed and to have the court so placed that litigants can with case and expedition take proceedings. The purpose of my moving this motion is to ascertain from the government whether it is proposed to take any steps to correct the difficulty of-which I complain, so that we shall have in connection with the Admiralty Court exactly the same opportunities of getting into the court as -we have in the other courts of the provinces. Although not a very old barrister, I remember when we had only two sittings of the Supreme Court in the county of Cape Breton. To-day we have seven sittings of that court, which shows how its business has enlarged. While the business of the Admiralty Court is enlarging in the same way, even more rapidly proportionately, we have in that court the same condition of things that we had 150 years ago, at the time the court was established. I think that every hon. member of this House will acknowl-edga that to be obliged to go 200 or 300 Mr. McKenzie.
miles to issue a writ in any court in this Dominion is rather behind the age, and that we cannot move too quickly in bringing about better conditions which will enable litigants more speedily to get their remedies in this court, which has exclusive jurisdiction in many matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the motion which the hon. gentleman has placed upon the Order Paper, there is, of course, no objection to the production of any such correspondence which may exist. The subject which my hon. friend has discussed in making the motion is one of very considerable practical importance. I may say at once that, so far as I am concerned, I have not in the least degree changed the opinions which I formed after a good deal of considefation of this matter, and which I stated to this House cn the 12th of March, 1908. I then introduced a resolution, which was considered in Committee of the Whole, declaring the expediency of making better provision for the exercise of admiralty jurisdiction within Canada, and upon that resolution being adopted in committee, I introduced a Bill founded upon it. That Bill was not pressed to a conclusion, but was dropped at the end of the session. The only reason, so far as I am concerned, why it was not pressed to a conclusion was the very strong objections to what was being proposed, which, on that occasion, were given utterance to by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House for whose opinions I had the most sincere respect. The general feeling, as I gathered it from the course of that debate, was against making any change, and, indeed, some hon. gentlemen_ expressed themselves as entirely content with the existing condition of things in the different provinces of the Dominion, and as thinking that no improvement could be made upon it.
I am sorry that I was not convinced by anything I heard on that occasion, and the three years which have passed since, with the experience they have given me of the working of the present system, have confirmed the opinion I then had formed, and which I then strongly expressed, namely, that existing conditions in the administration of justice in admiralty matters in Canada are simply intolerable. My hon. friend has instanced one circumstance which, if it were the only one, would seem to me now, as it did three years ago, to call for a remedy. Action has often to be taken and taken speedily. It is often a denial of justice to a man and the loss of his claim unless he can assert it, in admiralty matters particularly, with promptness and despatch, as the proceedings are frequently issued, not against the individual but against the ship, with the object of fastening the claim upon something tangible and secur-

ing judgment against the thing itself. A ship is here to-day and gone to-morrow. Wages to the men may be due; they may be unable to collect unless they can attach the ship and force payment in that way of what is justly due them by the owner. The ship may be a foreign vessel, it may be in port in Canada only a few hours, and unless you can serve process against the ship while she remains within Canadian jurisdiction, there may be no redress. But, under the present system proceedings cannot be instituted except through the post. You cannot attach by telegram, so that no matter where you may live, you must have your papers issued from the centre of the province to be served in the port, a process which may take 48 hours or longer. In the meantime the ship is gone, and your claim with it. That position of matters, if there were no other reason, did seem to me to call for a remedy ; and I thought that in the proposition to transfer the admiralty jurisdiction from the Exchequer Court to the various provincial courts, I had found a remedy. I was not able to understand the violent-I think I am not using any too strong a word-opposition which this proposition created among lawyers generally in the different larger centres in Canada where legal business would no doubt be more or less affected by the change I was proposing. That change, I must remind hon. gentlemen who were here at the time, was what I have just intimated, namely, simply the transfer of the admiralty jurisdiction to the various provincial courts so that every judge of a Superior Court in every province would be clothed with that jurisdiction, and so that a Surrogate Court or local judge, having authority to act in Superior Court matters, could be found in the person of every county judge in every province. The effect would be that any one desiring to institute proceedings in admiralty matters could do so in his own county town with the same facility with which he could issue an ordinary writ of summons for the enforcement of an ordinary civil claim. But the proposal was infringing upon what had been supposed to be a greater or less extent, the private preserves of this, that or the other local practitioner. It was interfering with existing conditions and vested rights ; it was going to take from a judge in one province or another some exclusive jurisdiction and hand that over generally to all the Superior Court judges in that province ; and accordingly every friend of every judge who would be effected by this measure, and every friend of every local registrar or clerk of court who might see a possible diminution in his salary was in arms against the suggestion ; and with regard to the local legal practitioner who
at present is compelled just because he cannot do this admiralty work in his own town or office, to send it to some provincial centre, all of the professional men in those provincial capitals were at once arrayed against this proposal which might cut into their incomes. It was too radical, it was wrong from every point of view, and the opposition offered both by friends and opponents in this House being all but unanimous, I was forced to think, in deference to the body of opinion which seemed to be against me, that I was altogether too radical and had better cease my efforts to become a law reformer. The Bill accordingly was not gone on with, and matters have remained in the same condition since 1908 that they were in since 1891. I think that is entirely anomalous, and if it appears, from .the course of the present debate, that the views of hon. gentlemen in this regard have changed, and that a measure such as I introduced three years ago would now receive a different sort of welcome, I shall be only happy to introduce it over again and submit it for consideration. I should like to say further that if it be remembered how the admiralty jurisdiction which is now vested in the Exchequer Court, came to be conferred upon that court, I think it will be seen at once that in the suggestion to transfer that jurisdiction to the various provincial courts there is nothing really radical. Until 1891 the admiralty jurisdiction had been exercised in Canada by the British Vice Admiralty 'Court, which might be, and probably was in each case, presided over by a judge who possessed by appointment from Canadian source the ordinary jurisdiction of Superior Courts in Canada, but who received his admiralty jurisdiction from England, and the procedure differed materially, when he was sitting in admiralty from that which existed when he happened to be sitting in the ordinary discharge of his duties as judge of ia Canadian court.
In 1890, the imperial parliament passed its Act by which jurisdiction was conferred upon colonial legislatures, if they saw fit, to alter that state of things; and the language of the Imperial Act passed in 1890, contemplated, as it seems to me, that the admiralty jurisdiction which was then being taken away from the British vice-admiralty courts in the various colonies should be conferred upon the ordinary courts of each colony by colonial legislation. Let me read the section of the British Act, which, as it seems to me, has that plain intendment:
Every court of law which may be declared to be a Court of Admiralty shall possess this jurisdiction, or, failing any such declaration, every court of law which has in a British possession original unlimited civil jurisdiction ' shall be a Court of Admiralty.

Now, if we had made in Canada no declaration on the subject-as we did make by the statute of 1891-then, under the Imperial Act, this admiralty jurisdiction would have gone just where by the Bill of three years ago I proposed to send it-namely to those courts which had original unlimited civil jurisdiction. But in 1891 this parliament passed its Act by which admiralty jurisdiction was conferred upon the Exchequer Court, the only federal court available, not a court which possessed original unlimited civil jurisdiction, but a special statutory court which had then recently been established. If any one will take the trouble to examine the debate upon that occasion, he will see how much Sir John Thompson, who was then Minister of Justice, hesitated. He states his hesitation with perfect candour to the House and with how slight an overbalancing of the hesitation it was he came to the conclusion to try the experiment of conferring this jurisdiction upon the new Exchequer Court which, at that time, I suppose-indeed, I know-had not very much of Exchequer Court business to do as compared with what it has to-day.
Well, now, the practical working out of the course which was then taken is that there must be a deputy of the judge of the Exchequer Court in certain localities in the Dominion. These deputies of the exchequer judge are local judges in admiralty of the Exchequer Court. There is one in Nova Scotia, one in Prince Edward Island, one in New Brunswick, one in Quebec, one in Ontario, one in British Columbia and one in the Yukon. The other provinces, having no maritime business to do, have never had a local judge in admiralty appointed. Now, in each of the provinces where there is a local judge in admiralty, the individual holding the position is either one of the judges of the Superior Court of the province or a retired judge of the Superior Court of the province. The proposition that I made was, not that there should be only one such judge in each province and that one a deputy of the judge in exchequer at Ottawa, but that there should be as many judges in admiralty in each province as there were judges in the Superior Court of that province, and that these judges should not be any retired judges of the court who had been superannuated, but the active working judges for the time being of the provincial Superior Court, the work to be divided among them and taken by them exactly as their ordinary'-work is divided, and as they would distribute among themselves the ordinary work of the courts which they were assigned to take, and that there should be in each instance a surrogate or local judge of the provincial court in the person of the county judge of each county in each province possessing the jurisdiction to do the ordinary practice work which such Sir ALLEN AYLESWOKTH.
judges now possess in the Superior Courts of the various provinces.
I was not able to understand the strong opposition which that proposition elicited; and I can only say that, in my humble judgment, the three years which have passed since then have made matters just three years worse. In some provinces, I think, there is to-day no practical difficulty. It would be invidious to particularize, but while it is the case that in some of the provinces everything is satisfactory, although all of the admiralty work is being done in each case by one judge instead of being distributed among all the members of the court, in other provinces, I am satisfied, things -are certainly in a very unfortunate position at the present time.

I would like to join with my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) who moved the resolution in expressing the opinion that the time has come when there should be an amendment of the law in regard to the admiralty jurisdiction and the carrying out of litigation before that court, if not all over Canada at least in the maritime provinces. It'is not necessary to supplement the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) who. has gone into the matter so fully, and who, if I understand him, expressed the opinion that there is ample cause for the amendment sought by my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). Certainly, so far as jurisdiction is concerned, there could be no anomaly in assigning to each one of the members of the Supreme Court of any one of our provinces, the right to deal with all questions which may ari'se in regard to shipping. There is no magic, there is no mystery, surrounding the law relating to shipping. I remember that the discussion on the Bill introduced by the Minister of Justice three years ago, some hon. members ventured to assert that there was some particular quality in the law relating to shipping, making it so different from any other branch of the law that the only way in which it could be satisfactorily administered was to assign to it a judge whose sole duty it would be to deal with this subject. Those who deal with the practice of the law must know that there are many branches of the law of which this could be said with at least equal truth. For instance, in regard to companies; the complications that have developed in the law relating to companies have been so great that it might be said with greater reason than in the case of the law relating to shipping that we should have a special judge to administer that law. To those engaged in shipping and those living in the seaport towns, the grievance arising out of this matter is a very real one, the present system giving rise to great difficulty and serious expense. Even after giv-

ing due weight to the arguments in the debate referred to against the change in the courts, I trust that the motion of my hon. friend from Cape Breton will be implemented and that this much desired re. form will be brought into effect.

So far as the operations of the matter referred to by the Minister of Justice are concerned, 1 should imagine that an easier remedy, or at ail events, a more effective remedy mignt be found than the one suggested. As 1 understood his argument in the first instance it related to the necessity of expedition in admiralty proceedings. He pointed out that a ship may be in a Canadian port for only a few days or hours, and he spoke of the delay which resulted from the necessity of obtaining a warrant from the central office. AH that could be avoided, it seems to me, by a change in the rules of the Exchequer Court, by the establishment of local offices in different parts of the province. So far as to the magnitude of the business is concerned, I do not remember the time in Nova Scotia and I am more familiar with conditions in that province than elsewhere, when the business could not be attended to by one judge in addition to the other work devolving upon him. I have had a good deal of experience in the work of the Exchequer Court and the Admiralty Court and I am bound to say I never had the slightest difficulty in effecting an arrest and I never had any special difficulty in getting any case heard in the Admiralty Court. In fact I have had just as much difficulty and just as much delay in respect of the ordinary every day business of the Exchequer Court of Canada as I have had in connection with the local Admiralty Court of the province of Nova Scotia.
I do not desire to again go over the arguments upon the Bill with which my hon. friend has dealt, at very great length. I know there was a great deal of opposition to the Bill which he introduced. Opposition developed in different quarters for different reasons. I fully appreciate the position taken by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member who introduced this motion that there ought to be no unusual or unnecessary delay in the Admiralty Court. I am prepared to go further and say that the Admiralty Court ought to be one in which cases could be proceeded with more expeditiously perhaps than in any other court in the country. It is so for the most part; in the Admiralty Court there are no nleadings. Within a few davs after a vessel has been seized and without any formal pleadings the case is set down for trial unless the court in its wisdom orders that pleadings shall be filed. Tor the most part the ease goes on without pleadings and without much delay
1 venture to suggest that a great deal of what my hon. iriend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has put forward as a grievance can be met by the establishment of local omces of the Admiralty uourt in the different provinces and by the appointing of deputy registrars. The conditions were not very much changed by the Act of 1891. Up to that time, in a great many provinces at least, the chief justice for the time being had been appointed by the imperial authorities to be the judge in admiralty. After the introduction of the Act of 1891 by Sir John Thompson the judge of me -tixcnequer Court oi Canada became the judge in admiralty, and he appointed the same men to be the local judges who had been acting before, at least in Nova Scotia, so that after all things went on very much as they had been going on in the past. The practice of file court was rendered simpler, but otherwise matters went on in very much the same way. I repeat that the appointing of a number of registrars would do a great deal to remove the inconvenience which has been alluded to this afternoon by the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie).

I do not rise to discuss the question from a legal point of view, but it appears to me that the Bill to which the Minister of Justice referred is the best remedy to apply. There is no reason, so far as I can judge, why there should not be every facility for dealing with such matters. I happen to represent the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William where there is a large amount of shipping, I believe larger than in any other port in Canada, taking the two cities together. There is a great deal of difficulty there. Time and again it has occurred that vessels could not be arrested and the remedy which ought to have been applied under the Admiralty Court could not be applied because of the distance from any jurisdiction in that regard. I think that matter has been referred to by the legal profession in those two cities and called to the attention of the Minister of Justice. I am sure the Minister of Justice is right and I hope he will have the courage of his convictions and go on and put the Bill through.

The remedy proposed by the. leader of the opposition will to some extent meet the particular grievance that we complain of in Nova Scotia, particularly in the eastern part of that orovince, but unless the Act will provide that the judge will go on circuit and try cases when ready for trial we would still be in verv much the same difficulty as before. Very of + on, we have as our witnesses in a case every member of the crew of a ship. It costs $30 a head of conduct money to take

witnesses from the town where I live, a seaboard town, to Halifax. If you have to take ten or twelve seamen it amounts to a large sum in trying a ease in Halifax.

It has been [DOT] the practice sometimes to take the evidence of such witnesses before a commission and thus obviate their being brought to Halifax. I know that is done in many cases and possibly it might be done still. But apart from that I would like to supplement my remarks by saying that I think there is no reason m the world why the judge should not go on circuit and try these cases.

The practice of taking evidence before a commission does not apply much more to trials in the Admiralty Court than in any other court. There is, of course, a provision under the judicature Act which differs very little from the practice of the Admiralty Court that the judge may order that the evidence may be taken before a commission and submitted to the judge. That applies, of course, perhaps with greater facility to admiralty cases but if it is objected to on the other side and a desire is expressed before the judge for the cross-examination of these witnesses before the judge himself I do not know that the order would be granted or that it would be permitted to examine witnesses in that way. Therefore, having the judge go on circuit, having the cases tried on the spot and as speedily as possible, because you cannot hold these witnesses for any great length of time, would be the best remedy. It is desirable to have facilities for issuing papers in the Exchequer Court as in any other and the trial in the ordinary way by a circuit judge.
I do not quite understand how my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bcrden), hesitates in agreeing to throw this jurisdiction into the Supreme Court of Neva Scotia. I think myself, that the tendency will be, to have a more competent better equipped court, than we have now. We would then have seven judges in admiralty with the ordinary life in the court which does not exist in any court when there is only one judge, and that one judge only dealing with admiralty as something subsidiary to his other business. I think, judging by the court we have to-day in Nova Scotia, it would be an exceptionally strong Admiralty Court, the practice being the same, the law not changed in any way whatever and a great part of the law being common to both courts. The law of evidence, the law of practice and procedure, and the law of damage is common to both courts and each of the judges being quite capable of trying a suit in admiralty, I can hardly understand why any lawyer from Nova Scotia should object at all to having the jurisdiction exercised by one of these Mr. McKENZIE.
judges exercised by each and every one of them. I would be in favour, of the Bill if the Minister of Justice will introduce it again and in that way I hope that such remedies as will give us improved conditions in the province, will be brought about. . I beg to move the motion.
Motion agreed to.

RICHARDS (Prince Edward Island), moved:	'
For a copy of all memorials, reports, correspondence and documents in the possession of the government, not already brought down, relating to a survey of a route for a tunnel under the Straits of Northumberland between the province of Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada, and also relating to the construction of such tunnel.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words upon this question before the motion is passed. It has been discussed upon several occasions very fully, especially during the last session of this parliament, when my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Warburton), gave us a great deal of information with regard to the necessity of such a work. In the province of Prince Edward Island, we are very often at a great disadvantage in consequence of not having regular means of communication. In a fertile island of that kind, productive as it is,, especially in its agricultural lands, the question of transportation is one of very great importance to us. It is true, that the winter steamers which we have in the service there, have been a considerable amount of help to us during the winter season in taking our products from the province to the mainland and other parts of' the continent, but during severe winters communication in that way is very irregular and uncertain, and it has, to a certain extent, a bad effect on the progress of the island from a commercial point of view. I am ready to give credit to the government for their good work in giving to the province that magnificent steamer, the * Earl Grey '. That boat was designed and built as an ice-breaker. She has done very good work and no doubt will do as-well as any boat of that kind can possibly do, but there are times when it is impossible for any ice-breaker, no matter how strongly she may be built, to keep up regular communication and during these times,
I feel that we are at a great disadvantage-in consequence of not having regular communication.
With reference to the tunnel, there are-some who, perhaps are disposed to treat this matter very lightly. But, it is a well known fact that tunnelling has made great advances in the world. There are many tunnels in the United States, in England and in other parts of Europe and the cost;

of tunnelling to-day is not nearly as great as it was some years ago. A great deal more information has been obtained with reference to the work of tunnelling and consequently, the cost has been greatly reduced. Considering this matter in that light, I think that we are entitled in the province of Prince Edward Island to have some steps taken with the view of making an investigation or survey of the proposed route for the tunnel. This is a question of so much importance that it will not down until some investigation or survey has been made, in order that the question of the practicability or otherwise of the work may be settled.
I do not intend this afternoon to go fully into all the particulars with regard to tunnelling ; that is to say, the size of the tunnel, the material of which it should be constructed or such things as that because those are matters that have already been brought before this House, and it would 'be a subject which would be taken up by those who would undertake to make the survey. My object on the present occasion is again to bring this matter to the attention of this parliament, and I hope that in my efforts in this regard I shall have the support of members from the other provinces. I feel that the construction of this work would not only be of advantage to the province from which I come, (but it would also be of great advantage to tire provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick. Quebec and, in fact, Ontario. It is not from the sectional point of view that I approach the discussion of this question. I look upon it as a question of national interest and importance. What benefits one province, especially with regard to the matter of allaying irritation and promoting harmony and good-will, is an advantage to all the provinces and, looking at the matter in this light, I think that we would expect that the people of the other provinces would give us their sympathy and support. I have understood that on some other occasions in this House, when this matter has been brought up for discussion, hon. members from the great province of Ontario Who know practically something about tunnels have given expressions of opinion favourable to the construction of this work between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
My object, as I have said, in bringing this matter before the House, is to again direct the_ attention of parliament to the great desirability of having some steps taken with a view to making a proper survey. It is true that a survey was made some few years ago, but I am told by engineers who are capable of passing an opinion upon such a subject that the ser-vey, though good as far as it goes, is not sufficient to enable anybody to make an
estimate as to the cost of the work. The position, as far as I can gather, that the people of Prince Edward Island take with reference to this matter is this : They say that if we have a survey made, and it is a proper survey, and it is found that the construction of this tunnel could be undertaken at something like a reasonable cost, at such an expenditure as we would have a right to expect the government would be justified in making, then, let us have it. If, on the other hand, it is shown by an investigation that this work is of such a magnitude, that its cost would be so great that this parliament would not be justified in making such a big expenditure for a province like Prince Edward Island, then the question will be settled, and there will be no more about it. But, until something of this kind is done there will be this agitation for the construction of this work, and I do sincerely hope that serious consideration will be given to this matter, that it will be taken up vigorously, and that such measures will be adopted that the question can be settled as to whether the construction of a tunnel between Prince Edward Island and the mainland is a practicable work or whether it is not.
From the information that I have been able to obtain from engineers who have had experience in work I am led to believe that, such a project may be practicable, but that it will be difficult to make an estimate of its cost until -a survey has been made. If that work can be constructed for $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 I think the parliament of Canada would be amply justified in making such an appropriation to afford to the smallest province of this great Dominion regular and continuous communication both winter and summer with the mainland. I could say a very great deal more on this important question, but I think I have said sufficient to-call the attention of the government to the desirability of taking steps towards having a proper and thorough survey made in connection with the tunnel project.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to say a few words on this subject, which is not new to the House, and which in the past has been often and ably advocated. I shall not go at length into the subject, but I may say to those people who have expressed an opinion that the country would not be justified in building this tunnel at all on account of the cost, that they do not exactly know what they are talking about. However that may be, what the people of Prince Edward Island want now, and what they have been asking for years is that a survey be made to determine the estimated cost. If the cost is so large as to be unreasonable and unjustifiable, then the people of Prince

Edward Island would not press their claim. But, Sir, the people of my province make a fair and reasonable request when they ask the government to provide money for a survey. I spoke on this point last year, and I was answered by the Minister of Finance in the following words, which I shall quote from page 290 ' Hansard,' vol. I, 1909-10. These words of the Finance Minister, when circulated in our province, raised the hopes of many people that the survey would be proceeded with at once, but, unfortunately for us, nothing has been done. I quote from Mr. Fielding:-
I am glad to hear my hon. friends from the island say that all they ask is that this matter shall be thoroughly and impartially inquired into, and if the tunnel can be built at a moderate cost they think the work should be done. To that sentiment I most heartily subscribe, and I am quite sure that the government will have that feeling towards,it. There have been some surveys in the past. ' I suppose that each of them in its day served the purpose, it was the best that could be had; but I quite agree with my hon. friends that the matter should be taken up more vigorously and more seriously, and that we should endeavour to get a reliable and thorough survey by the best engineers, and if, as a result of that survey, it is found that this important work can be constructed at a moderate cost, I for one, would promise my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island my most hearty and cordial support.
The Minister of Finance made this statement on the 22nd of November, 1909, in the early days of last session, and his announcement that the matter would be taken up vigorously and seriously led the people to think that last summer steps would be taken to begin this survey. I regret to say that the government are not entitled to claim any very great praise for the way in which they have since dealt with this question. The Minister of Finance told us it should be taken up seriously, and yet we are well on into the present session and the main estimates for next year are down and theTe is not one cent included in them for this tunnel survey. I would not like to accuse the government of holding this matter back until the next election, but I am afraid some people will be suspicious that the government is waiting until the approaching elections to take the matter up seriously and vigorously. I urge now that a sum of money be placed in the supplementary estimates of this year for the beginning of the survey, and that the government should proceed with the work without further delay.

Mr. Speaker, last session I had the honour of bringing this question myself before this House, and as I went into the question at considerable length and in great detail, I shall not speak at any great length to-day.

The question has been a sort of hardy annual before the House for many years, and unfortunately a great many people had come to took upon it, not in the serious light which it deserves. That, I think, is due to the manner in which this important question has been placed before the country in the past, by some well intentioned, but indiscreet, advocates in the press, on the platform, and in parliament. Owing to these ill-directed efforts this great scheme became, to some extent, 1 am sorry to say, a matter of more or less ridicule. At the first session of the present parliament, when I entered this House, 1 noticed this state of affairs, and in consultation with my colleagues we decided not to bring the matter before the House at that first session, but that the wiser course was to drop it for the time being, so that the absurd impression which had been created should be allowed to die out. I am glad to think that my anticipation in this regard has to some extent c.ome to pass, and that now the people of Canada and the members of this parliament look upon the Prince Edward Island tunnel scheme in a more serious light than they formerly did. I shall not refer to. the survey made 20 years ago by Sir Douglas Fox, further than to point out that in speaking of t,he method of the survey which he thought ought to be carried on before the government undertook the work, he was careful to state, in giving his estimate of the cost upon such data as he had before him, that this estimate would be likely to change as a result of more complete information than was then in his possession. He pointed out that the proper course would be to take the line across the straits, where it was proposed to build the tunnel, and then, taking two lines parallel with the centre line at a distance of 300 yards on either side, to bore hol-ss along these lines through the underlying strata at intervals of 500 yards, so as to discover what the material was through which the tunnelling would have to be done. All that we ask at the present moment is that this recommendation of Sir Douglas Fox, or something similar to it, should be carried out. I wish it to be distinctly understood that at the present time we are not asking the government or the country to build a tunnel. Whenever we mention this matter in this House it is published in the newspapers that we are asking,the government to build a tunnel. But, again, I wish it to be understood that what we are now asking is that a survey should be made to determine whether a tunnel is practicable or not. That, I think, is a very reasonable request. Owing to the supposed geological formation of red clay shale on a carboniferous or gray sandstone basis, said to contain small masses of fine standstone, it is said that there are likely to be fissures, and, therefore, a prime consideration in the question

of cost would be as to how much water would percolate through these fissures if there are such. It is said that if there are no fissures there will be no difficulty in building the tunnel, and hence the absolute .necessity for a careful and complete survey.
A very large proportion of the cost of this great undertaking will depend upon the nature of the ground through which the tunnel has to pass-not with regard to the difficulty of boring, but with regard to the difficulty of keeping out the water; and the great object of a survey is to ascertain whether there are any such fissures. This shale overlies a sandstone base, which it is believed continues for about one-fourth of the distance; so that if fissures were found to exist in the sandstone, the amount of water they would admit into the tunnel would be a most important factor in the whole distance, according to Sir Douglas Fox. My hon. friend from Kings county, has put this matter very briefly, but very well, and I am not going to take up the time of' this House in going into it in detail, as I thought I was justified in doing last session. I wish simply to try to impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, and this House the very great importance of this subject of transportation to Prince Edward Island. There is no province of the Dominion, not even excepting the western provinces, to which that subject is of so much importance; and if the question of a tunnel can be taken up and settled one way or the other, it will be of great advantage. If it is found to be practicable, it will be of great advantage to have the tunnel. If it is found to be impracticable, it will be of great advantage to have the question removed from the public arena.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it would be possible to give to our hon. friends from Prince Edward Island any stronger assurance of the sympathy Which the government has for this most important project than was conveyed in the language of my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), at the last session of parliament, when he used these words:-
I am glad to hear my hon. friend from the island say that all they ask is that this matter shall be thoroughly and impartially inquired into and if the tunnel can be built at a moderate cost they think the work should be done. To that sentiment I most heartily subscribe, and I am quite sure that the government will have that feeling towards it. There have been some surveys in the past. I suppose that each of them in its day served the purpose, it was the best that could be had; but I quite agree with my hon. friends that the matter should be taken up more vigorously and more seriously, and that we should endeavour to get a reliable and thorough survey by the best engineers, and if, as a result of that survey, it is found that this important work can he constructed at a moderate cost, I for one, would promise my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island my most hearty and cordial support.
I have no reason, Sir, to suppose that the views which -were presented by the Minister of Finance on that occasion, are any different from those which are entertained by the government as a whole. The question, however, of making a survey is a very important one. There is no use of making further surveys unless they are more thorough and complete than the surveys which have been made in the past. Speaking for myself personally, I would say that if a company were formed, which would undertake to build a tunnel between Prince Edward Island and the mainland for the sum which has been mentioned, $10,000,000, I .would favour the granting of that aid for the purpose. The difficulty, however, as presented to me by the engineers of my department, is that a tunnel may cost $10,000,000 or it may cost $40,000,000, depending upon whether fissures should be encountered in the progress of the work, and let in water from the ocean, which would enormously increase the cost. Anybody who has made a study of tunnels, even through mountains, on dry land, realizes how difficult it is accurately to estimate the cost and the difficulty is, of course, enormously increased, in the ease of a tunnel under water. Therefore, when a survey is undertaken, it is necessary that it should be undertaken under tire guidance of the most competent .and , experienced engineers, and that it should be thorough and complete covering almost every foot of tire distance between the mainland and the island. I can assure my hon. friends that the matter which has already been engaging the attention of my department, will be seriously considered, and I am not without hope, that provision will, before long, be made for a thorough and complete survey, which will be entirely satisfactory to our friends from Prince Edward Island.
Has the government ascertained anything as to the probable cost of a complete" survey P

Only in a general way. A complete survey would be pretty costly; but still, upon the information I have, I think the cost would not be regarded by parliament as larger than would be warranted by the great importance of the work, in case it should be possible to undertake it.
Can the hon. minister give us any idea of the time at which he intends to take up this work of the survey ?
I intend to submit the matter for the consideration of the government during the present session.

I may say, that at least three years ago, I am not sure that it was not four years ago, I strongly urged upon the government to do this very thing. I stated then that the people of Prince Edward Island and the people of the whole of the Dominion of Canada were entitled to know whether this was a practicable project or not, that ample time had already elapsed during which that information might have been obtained, and that, in my opinion, not a single day ought to be lost in taking effective steps for the purpose of enabling the government to place on the table of this House definite and specific information on this question. I entertain the same opinion to-day. I only regret that three or four years have been lost between that time and the present in which this work has not been taken up.
Motion agreed to.

TAYLOR (New Westminster), moved:	.
For a copy of all correspondence since the 1st of January, 1910, with the Department of Justice or any officers of that department, making or supporting request for increase of pay to employees of the penitentiary at New Westminster; and of all reports or recommendations in that connection made by any officer of the department. Also a copy of all reports made during the period indicated by the grand jury at New Westminster with reference to the conditions at said penitentiary.
He said: My object is to bring to the attention of the government and the House the very unsatisfactory situation of the officials of the penitentiary at New Westminster. The subject of the pay of these officials is not new to the government because for two or three years they have been making most persistent efiorts to get an increase which will to some extent put them on a level with their much better situated neighbours in the city of New Westminster. They have been encouraged by government officials to believe that their petitions were receiving serious consideration, and that in a short time they might expect good results, but the years have gone on the conditions of their labour have continued the same and their responsibilities and expenses have increased, and still, .hough the necessity for their being paid higher wages has increased, nothing has transpired to warrant the belief that they are any nearer success now than when they began to petition. In the meantime public attention has been directed to the conditions in that institution. We had a few years ago a report, a most unfair report, from an official at Ottawa referring to irregularities [DOT]in that penitentiary, and claiming that these showed inattention, neglect or perhaps incapacity on the part of the officers, Mr. PUGSLEY.
notwithstanding the fact that the officers had petitioned in vain for efficient help, and also to have the conditions of those who were employed made tolerable. We have had the matter brought before the public in a new and in a very formal manner in a report made by the grand jury at the city of New Westminster, in which report the attention of the government was invited to the conditions at the penitentiary, and which declared that these conditions were such as to invite and facilitate the escape of every prisoner confined in it. No doubt the Department of Justice has taken cognizance of that report and has resolved on some line of policy; but so far as the officials at the penitentiary are concerned, they have heard nothing whatever of anything being done for the purpose of providing a remedy and removing the reproach which the grand jury has fastened upon that institution. In bringing this matter before the House, I am anxious to impress upon hon. members as forcibly as I can, the fact that there is not in the minds of the public at New Westminster, any reproach upon the penitentiary officials. The view taken locally of that institution is that there is indeed a lack of that efficiency which we have the right to expect, but that this is due to the fact that the rate of pay offered by the department makes it impossible for those in charge to secure the class of help which they desire in order to carry out its work effectively. They find their old hands constantly leaving to accept more lucrative employment outside; they find the material available to fill the vacancies consists only of persons temporarily out of employment who take that service merely as a means to obtaining better positions outside it later. I am well aware that the conditions at New Westminster are not confined to that city but are common to all the penitentiaries in the west, and to a lesser degree, to those in the east; but the conditions at Westminster are accentuated by the excessive cost of living as compared with the east, and by the failure of the department to make a proportionate allowance to equalize these conditions.
I have had prepared a statement from the figures presented in the ' Labour Gazette ' of the cost of living in different places in Canada. I find that, as compared with eastern cities having penitentiaries, the cost of living in New Westminster is 51 per cent higher than at St. John, N.B., the point of comparison for Dorchester penitentiary, and 56 per cent higher than at Kingston. There is allowed to the lower officials west of Ontario $100 per year in consideration of their location, but this is absorbed absolutely by the difference in rent between New Westminster and the eastern cities. The table of rents.

as shown by the statistics in the ' Labour *Gazette 5 shows that at St. John, the nearest town to Dorchester quoted in these statistics, the average working man pays $9 per month, at Kingston he pays $10 per month, while at New Westminster the lowest at which any of the staff of the penitentiary can secure a house is $18 per month. So you will see that the difference in rental between the east and the west absorbs the whole of the extra allowance and leaves nothing to compensate for the extra cost of living in other respects.
This matter of salary is regulated, I believe, by statute, and therefore, cannot be so readily adjusted as if the conditions were otherwise. But I see in the estimates a move on the part of the Minister of Inland Revenue to deal with the officials of that department west of Ontario by providing a special allowance of $150 a year for every employee below a certain amount. I would suggest that a similar course should be followed with regard to the New Westminster penitentiary and other institutions, pending a more thorough statutory adjustment which might well be made in the shape of a general increase in the salaries of the officials of those institutions. There is no purpose to be served by dwelling at any length on this matter, but I would ask the minister whether he cannot give some indication to these men to encourage them and their families to hope that there is a ray of light ahead of them.

In this connection I would like to say a word or two regarding the institution at Stony Mountain. The employees there occupy very much the same position as those at Westminster. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has put the case so well before the House that I need not say more than that 1 heartily concur in the opinions and sentiments expressed by him. The hon. Minister of Justice, has, I believe, received a petition from the employees of the Stony Mountain penitentiary drawing his attention to some of the facts in Manitoba similar to those described by my hon. friend from Westminster as existing there'
As everybody is aware who knows anything about western life, the cost of living is very much higher in the west than in the east. We also know that men occupying the position, for instance, of instructors in these institutions command, as a rule, very much larger wages outside than are received from the government. Men occupying positions similar to those of instructors in the Stony Mountain institution receive in Manitoba any where from $5 to $6 or $7 a day; and I understand that these men are working for the government for something like $2.50 a dav. This, surely. should not be continued, and I enter
a plea with the Minister of Justice to consider the position of these men, taking into consideration at the same time the fact that they must be men of ability to instruct those who are placed under their charge, and of a good deal of force of character to command the respect of those whom it is their duty to instruct. And that they have been successful is evidenced by many of the men who have been turned out of that institution in Manitoba. The class of instructors the government has secured for that institution, 1 am glad to say, is perhaps as high as that in any other institution in Canada. They are worthy of every consideration the government can show them. I urge upon the government the desirability of treating the instructors and others in these institutions fairly liberally to encourage them to take an interest in their duty by showing them that the country appreciates what they are doing for the unfortunates who are placed under their care.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I
may at once state that I sympathize very sincerely with the views which have been expressed by both the hon. gentlemen who have discussed this motion. It is no longer ago than this morning that, at the breakfast table, I heard a discourse which was very eloquent and moving upon this very subject of the increased cost of living. And I scarcely know what the solution of the difficulty is to be. I think, however, that I can assure my hon. friends of the west that it is not alone in their part of the country that these difficulties are felt. Possibly, we shall continue to have them until the views of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) prevail, and we get rid of the increased price of commodities by getting rid of our tariff. Then, I suppose, we shall have nothing to pay except our taxes. And if we can manage to meet the taxes, the increased cost of living, possibly, will not be one of the things troubling every one who has to depend upon a fixed salary.
Now, with regard to the particular motion that is made here, there is certainly no objection to bringing down all the papers which exist and which are referred to in the motion. There is not, so far as I am aware, any presentment from a grand jury such as is referred to in the motion. I certainly have no recollection of seeing any such document within the last twelve months. But, upon the other branch of what is asked for, the application for increase of salaries of officials in the penitentiary at New Westminster, there have been urgent representations made during the last few months, and I have been for a longer period than that aware from the practical administration of affairs in the penitentiary that conditions are not satisfactory. Exactly what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor,

New Westminster) mentions is taking place. We need good men, reliable men, men of good physical as well as mental' qualifications, for the responsible position of guards in our penitentiaries. But such men can get better wages outside than they can get in the service, and the result is very generally that we no sooner get a good, capable man acquainted with his duties than some one else comes along and offers him more, and, of course, he takes it and we lose the man who has just learned to be valuable. But, while that is so, the practical question of what is to be done is far from being free from difficulty. The increased cost of living, as I said, seems not to be at all confined to the west. We have just as strong representations, just as numerous and emphatic representations, from our penitentiaries in the maritime provinces and in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and these * representations have been so unanimous from each one of our six penitentiaries and there has been so much practical difficulty In securing anything like permanency of service, of our guards particularly, that the question has become one which, I am afraid, cannot be any longer put off from practical consideration. I had been sanguine, when I took up the duties of the Department of Justice four years ago that this question, so far as the penitentiaries were concerned, would probably not' need to be considered again during my tenure of office. It was the first piece of work, I think, to which I fell heir when I took charge of the Department of Justice, to have in hand before the Committee of the Whole in this House the newly revised Penitentiaries Act which was passed in 1906. By that statute, a very considerable general increase in salaries was given. There was an effort to make that uniform. I think that effort was in the right direction. I should like to see the salaries uniform. It is difficult to satisfy the man from Nova Scotia or New Brunswick that his services in thd penitentiary are not worth just as much as those of the *man in identically the same position at Stony Mountain or New Westminster. And it is a very invidious sort of thing to make a distinction upon any such ground as that the cost of living is higher in one section of the country than in another. If it is to be recognized as right in the penitentiary service, it must follow in all branches of the service, and with the service to the .country worth just as much in one part of the Dominion as in another, it is difficult to justify upon principle the making of any distinction.
In respect to what is to be done about it, I cannot*give any other answer than to say, and I do say in all sincerity, that the subject is receiving, -and will continue to receive, the most careful consideration of which I am capable. It is one which does Sir ALLEN AYLESWOBTH.
not rest altogether with me, perhaps not at all _ with me; it is something in respect to which I must procure the assent of my colleagues to any recommendation I may make and, of course, the assent of this House. These salaries are fixed by statute. If the time has come, notwithstanding that it is only four years since there was an increase, it is for this House to say so, and if I can see my way to a recommendation which will to some extent .alleviate the condition of things which has been spoken of loy hon. gentlemen this afternoon and which in the practical everyday administration of the department, I certainly have very acutely felt for months, if not for years, I shall personally be only too glad.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster), moved:

For a copy of all correspondence between the Department of the Interior or any of its officers and any other persons, respecting the timber on the Fanny Louise Irwin homestead in the district of Chilliwack, British Columbia, including any instructions to solicitors to issue a writ in Exchequer Court for cancellation of timber rights not reserved in Crown grant of the homestead.
He said: I wish in a very few words to call attention to what I regard as a bluff on the part of the Department of Justice, but which while it does not appear serious to me is giving a great deal of uneasiness to the farmers in the district of Chilliwack against whom it is directed. The story at the foundation of this motion, is told in a couple of official letters summarized in this communication from the legal firm of Davis, Marshall & Macneil, of Vancouver, addressed to William R. Barge, of Rosedale. That letter reads:-
In January, 1910, you purchased from Mrs. Jane E. Hermon 10 acres of land, being part of the northeast quarter-section 31, township
2.	Mrs. Hermon purchased this property from Fanny Louise Irwin, who in turn obtained it from the Crown in August, 1903. The Department of Justice have instructed their solicitors at Ottawa to bring an action against you and the other holders of this property to have the patent issued, cancelled on the ground that it was issued in error, and should have reserved to the government the timber upon the lands in question. We have been asked by the solicitors for the Department at Ottawa to endeavour to come to some amicable arrangement with the owners before they issue a writ in the Exchequer Court against you.
The proposal made by the department is for the owners to agree to surrender the patent in question, upon the understanding that the Crown will issue a fresh patent reserving the timber. Would you be prepared to do this? Kindly let us know at once, os failing to hear from you, or should you re-

fuse, proceedings will be commenced in the Exchequer Court against yon.
I have another letter to the same effect from the same firm addressed to Mrs. .T, E. Hermon.
If the Department of Justice were dealing with the original patentee of this land, there might be some sense in these proceedings, because so long as the original patentee held something to which he was not legally entitled, it would be proper for the department to endeavour to overtake the error it had made, and to remedy the error; but in this case you find that several years have elapsed, these properties have passed into 16 or 20 hands; the first patentee of 160 acres, as I believe,	divided the property
into about four sections, each of these subdivided it and they have continued to subdivide it since, and now all these persons are menaced by a threat from the Department of Justice to take proceedings in the Exchequer Court to assail the rights which they obtained by virtue of a patent from the Department of the Interior to the original holder of these lands. I do not think that these persons have anything to fear from the Department of Justice or any other department of the government if they stand uj)on their rights. I do not think the department will ever go to the Exchequer Court with a case of that kind; I do not think they would last long if they did, and I say that in all humility as the opinion of a layman upon a point of law. I say further that the Department of the Interior should not be a party to this, they should be ashamed, to permit another department to issue this bluff against innocent persons, who had nothing whatever to do with the mistake in question, who had no possible means of knowing that any mistake had occurred, but who, on the contrary, owing to the conditions surrounding the timber in the Chilliwack district, had every reason to believe that this patentee who held the patent in her hand not reserving from the land the timber rights was indeed the owner, of the timber as so many settlers in that locality are the owners of the timber. This matter having been brought out in this way, _ I think it would be opportune for the Minister of the Interior to give some assurance to these settlers that they will not be harassed in this matter by the government, but that the responsibility for the error will be placed where it belongs, in the Interior Department, instead of, _ being visited on the heads of this large number of innocent persons in the Chilliwack district.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The case to which my hon. friend alludes is, in fact, as he has stated it. At one time, many years ago, it was the custom, to allow homestead entry upon timber lands in the province of British Columbia, excluding timber from the right of the homesteader and when the patent was issued to the homesteader, the timber was excluded from the patent. In this particular case, which my hon. friend has mentioned, and I think in one^ther case that has come to the attention of the Department of the Interior, the patent was issued to the homesteader without the reservation of the right to the timber.
The department, of course has no knowledge of what disposition has been made of his rights, or her rights, by the patentee but the department is perfectly aware that the original owner of the timber is still the owner of the timber and, in dealing with the matter, the effort has been made to secure to the holder of the timber the rights which he paid for, and which he possesses, that is, the right to cut the timber upon this land, a right of which the homesteader was perfectly aware at the time that the homestead entry was given, and, of course, at the time the patent was issued. Instead of the present holders of the land being willing to accept a patent for the land excluding the timber, according to the equity of the case, they have seen fit to stand upon what they are pleased to consider their legal rights. Holding a patent which does not exclude the timber, they refuse to give up the timber. It was a legal matter, and was left by the Department of Interior to that of justice. On the advice of the Department of Justice proceedings were being taken to reinstate the respective parties to their rights according to the conditions upon which they had been parted with. In so far as the Department of Interior is concerned, we are anxious not to do anything that will oppress or injure any individual settler, or the purchaser from an individual settler, but, on the other hand, the department is anxious to protect rights which it has passed to other individuals, and which by error have not otherwise been protected. If my hon. friend asks for an apology from the Department of Interior for the action taken, I can only say that I do not see that any apology can be offered, except that an apology might be offered by the officials of the government who made the error, which government I may say, was our predecessor in office ; hut, for the action of this government in doing what can be done to protect the rights of the owners of the timber, who have unquestionably the right in equity to the timber, I do not think that there is any apology to be offered.
Was there a license on the timber when the patent was issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and when the homestead was given also.
I would like to ask the minister if the letter written by the Vancouver solicitors was written with the authority or by the instruction of the Department of Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not answer that .unless I saw the letter.
It is the letter which my ,hon. friend from New Westminster has just read.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would have to refer to the records of the department. I could not answer off-hand.

The letter, I see, states that they have authority from the government to take proceedings in the Exchequer 'Court. I can only say that this is the ordinary, usual case of a bona tide purchaser for value without notice, and it is recognized in all the courts in the land that a person who gets a title in that way has a perfect title. I think it is idle for the Minister of the Interior to say that the department are justified in instructing a firm of solicitors to endeavour to recover from those parties, who have innocently purchased in good faith and paid full consideration, any compensation whatever because of the two they are the innocent parties. But here, notwithstanding that this letter states that if these innocent, bona fide purchasers for value, do not do as thei department suggest-that is release the right to the timber, I suppose-action will be taken in the Exchequer Court of Canada. In the first place, I submit that no action can 'be taken as a matter of law and that as a matter of equity it should not be taken, and therefore, the department has no right to put up a bluff of this kind against innocent purchasers.

The department seems to be very much more zealous in this case than it was in the case of the Blairmore townsite. There a grant had been procured from the Crown by the grossest fraud and imposition, proved by evidence, and found by the judgment of the Exchequer Court of Canada. Notwithstanding that fact, the department recalled the judgment of the court after it had been pronounced, took no further proceedings, and left those in possession of the property on whose behalf the fraud and imposition had been practised.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I may have the privilege, I would like to point out a very wide difference between the two cases. In the case under discussion of the patent of Fanny Louise Irwin, if it were merely a question between the government and Mrs. or Miss Irwin, there would be no attempt on the part of the department to cancel the patent which had been issued.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not an attempt to assert the right of the Crown to this property ; it is an attempt to protect the right of the proper owner of the timber upon that property, which right he has not disposed of, which we have no right to take from him and cannot take from him, and which the owner of this property knows perfectly well that he or she has no equitable right to. Because of an error in the issue of the patent, which, I repeat, was not the fault of the present administration, they hope to secure a value in the timber that does not belong to the Crown but belongs to another private person.

I think there is a very great difference between the two cases, but for the reason that I pointed out, and not for the reason that the minister has assigned. In the Blairmore town-site case action was taken 'by the Attorney General of Canada upon the relation of a man who was entitled to the property as against the Crown. That man proved his case in court. He was the relator in the suit at whose instance the Attorney General of Canada took that proceeding. His case proved up to the hilt that fraud and imposition had resulted in the title passing from the Crown to some other person. That was absolutely proved by evidence, and that was found by the judgment of the judge of the Exchequer Court. Notwithstanding all that the Crown put to one side the man who had proved his case in court and directed that no further proceedings should be taken against the men who had received the benefit of the fraud and imposition that had been practised upon the Crown and which had been described in very emphatic and distinct terms not only by the judge in the west, Mr. Justice Wetmore, to whom the matter had been referred for the purpose of taking the evidence, but also by tire then judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, Mr. Justice Burbidge. I think there is a difference between the two cases, but I do not think it is a difference that would impel the government to take action in the present case when they had refrained from action in the case to which I have alluded.

Mr. Speaker, .1 would like to correct a couple of errors into which the Minister of the Interior appears to have fallen. In the first place he said that the mistake, if any, was not of this administration but of their predecessors. I wish to call attention to the fact that the mistake was made in 1903 when this administration was in office as it is now. Next, the minister stated on two occasions, that these persons perfectly well knew they had not the rights to which they so tenaciously held. 1 am in a position to say to the minister

that he has no warrant for that belief, that as a matter of fact the present owners, or some of them whom 1 know, had no reason whatever to suppose that they were not the absolute proprietors of this timber when they bought the lands under the deed giving that right to the persons from whom they purchased. I am in a position to say further, that one of the persons to whom this threat was addressed had actually resold his right before he was ordered by the department to surrender his patent.
