He would have been in the position of having to compensate the person to whom he had sold, but without anv recourse himself. I have another letter here which I will read to round off the correspondence, and this letter covers one or two of the points unintentially mis-stated by the minister. It is dated April 13, 1910. and addressed to Mrs. Jane E. Hermon, Rose-dale P.O., B.C., I would like to lay emphasis upon the chivalry of a department that will attack a helpless woman in this manner. The letter goes on:
Dear Madam,-In August, 1903, the Crown granted to Fanny L. Irwin certain lands in the railway belt in the province of British Columbia. On the 20th of November, 1909, the lands were conveyed to you by Fanny L. Irwin-
So that, as you will see, the department very well knew that she was not the original homesteader:
-subsequently you sold a portion to Joseph W. Oakes and a portion to William Robert Barge. Apparently from the documents in the land registry office you still have an interest in a portion of this property. The Dominion government have instructed proceedings to be taken in the Exchequer Court of Canada against you and the other owners to cancel this patent on the ground that it was issued in error as the timber should have been reserved from the lands in question. Messrs. Chrysler, Betliune & Larmonth, of Ottawa, are acting for the Crown in this matter and have asked us to see if some amicable arrangement cannot be arrived at with the owners before commencing legal proceedings. The proposition made is that the parties now entitled to the property should surrender their patent to the Crown.
Mark the words: ' now entitled to the property; ' that is what these lawyers said:
The proposition made is that the parties now entitled to the property should surrender their patent to the Crown, on the understanding that a new patent shall issue reserving the timber. Kindly let us hear whether you would be prepared to consent to such an arrangement.
Yours faithfully,
DAVIS, MARSHALL, MACNEIL & PUGH.
So, here we find an answer to the minister's statement that this was done by his Tory predecessors when as a fact it was 70
done in 1903, and also to his statement that the department were dealing with parties who very well knew they had no rights. His own solicitor's letter actually refers to this long series of transfers. I think it is a most astounding thing that the government of a great country like Canada should presume upon the ignorance of settlers in a remote part of the Dominion to think that these settlers would accept a bluff of this kind, and at a cost of hundreds of dollars to each of them, enable the department to find an easy way out of an error which it had committed.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster), moved:
For a copy of all correspondence between the Post Office Department and any of its officials or other persons, relative to making an allowance for the transportation of letter carriers on the tramway system in New Westminster.
He said: I am happy to say that since I put this notice on the paper its object has been accomplished by the issue of an order for the payment of the transportation of the letter carriers. However, if the minister has no objection I think it is well that the motion should carry because there was very extraordinary delay in securing this little concession, and I should like to know why this delay occurred.

I have no objection to the papers being brought down. I may tell my hon. friend that there was no ill-will on the part of the department towards paying for the transportation of the letter carriers, but we thought at the time there was a combine between the street railway companies of the various cities to claim an exorbitant amount for this service. We did not object to pay the transportation of the letter carriers in these cities, but at the same time we did not wish to pay the street railway companies an exorbitant amount. We were always willing to pay a moderate price. The reason of the delay was that we were conducting negotiations with the various street railway companies of the cities from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Motion agreed to.

MONK (Jacques Cartier), moved for:-
A return showing in detail:-
1. All sums paid by the concessionnaires of grantees of the Beauharnois canal as rental or royalties upon the rights conveyed to them by the Crown on the Beauharnois canal, or paid by their assigns in the enjoyment of the said rights, since the concession.



2.	Of all sums paid oi' expended by the government upon the said canal since the date of the said concession.
3.	Of all sums actually due the Crown by the grantees or assigns for the use of said canal or in connection therewith.
He said: The object of this motion is to put the House in possession of all the facts and circumstances connected with the alienation of the Beauharnois canal. Some of these papers were brought down some time ago, but I have not been able to find them, and it is important at, this juncture that we should become familiar with the facts, as there is now before the House a Bill to regulate the method of the alienation of our water-powers. 1 presume there is no objection to our obtaining this information. I may add that we have just had held in the city of Quebec a forestry and conservation meeting, at which the resources of this country have been discussed and enumerated and enlarged upon as never before. We were told there of the vast extent of our forest wealth, and it was asserted by those who are competent to speak upon the subject, that there was to be found in Canada probably 40 per cent of all the water-powers in the world. The importance of husbanding these resources and of alienating them only after the observance of most careful formalities, were subjects fully treated of at that meeting in Quebec. It is very important that we should know the extent of our resources, but it seems to me it is equally essential that we should do something practical towards their conservation, or otherwise the circumstances which have attended their alienation in the past would soon leave us without these resources. There were some guiding principles laid down at the Quebec meeting, which do not seem to have been observed when the government parted with the Beauharnois canal. The principle was admitted on all hands that none of our water-powers or other resources ought to be rented or alienated without, in the first place, the preparation of a careful estimate of what the particular object to be alienated consists of and upon what terms such alienation should take place. I have been unable to discover that this rule was observed when we parted with the Beauharnois canal. There was not a carefully prepared estimate of what that canal represented in the way of capital expenditure, what we should claim as a return upon that capital expenditure, what the future worth of the water-power to the surrounding country might be, and what we received as a return for that alienation. No such careful estimate was made before the property was alienated. There was no provision made in the deed of alienation for an increase of rental in case the waterpower of the Beauharnois canal should be increased bv subsequent work on the part of the concessionnaires in order to derive a Mr. MONK.
larger revenue than was anticipated. There was no publicity before the alienation took place. There was no general invitation for tenders in order to ascertain whether others v ere ready to give more for that valuable pioperty than was given finally by those who acquired it. That was another condition which is insisted upon not only in the laws and regulations of all tne other countries that have dealt with the alienation of water-powers, but by all those on this continent who have studied the question. Here was a valuable water-power situated within reach of several important centres, and within easy reach of the city of Montreal. Indeed, I believe that it is at present intended to use that water-power to supply the city of Montreal with electricity. A vast field was thus opened to those who had the handling of the power, and no tenders were asked for. The alienation, I understand, was a perpetual one. On this matter there has not been much legislation in Europe, but there has been some in Switzerland and in France, and I believe attempts have been made to get legislation in the United States. There was no provision, as I understand, for a revision of the rentals from time to time. I speak without having seen the deed. The original grantee of the powers has, I understand, transferred his privileges.
In what year was the grant made?
I do not know exactly in what year, but I think four or five years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About five years ago.

So that, as far as we know, none of the principles which it is claimed everywhere should apply to such alienations from the state were observed in the alienation of the Beauharnois canal. I remember that my hon. friend paid a visit to Beauharnois at the time there was a rumour-abroad that the alienation was about to take place, but I am not aware that rival parties were given a chance to make an offer, which I believe would have been superior to the one which was accepted by the government. At all events, it is conceded by those who know about the transaction that it has been immensely profitable to the grantees. I hope we shall have no more of such alienations. I hope that even at the present session the government will adopt some legislation which will, for the future, prevent any indiscriminate alienation of a most valuable asset. I cannot but believe that there is exaggeration in the statement, made by competent persons, however, that we have in Canada 40 per cent of the water-powers of the world, but even if we have a far less proportion of the world's wealth, it is evident that we

must, be careful of it, and that we must not merely announce the policy of conservation, but put it into practical shape, so that governments can never in the future be tempted to make such alienations as the one referred to in this motion. We can, of course, only speak fully as to the facts when the return is brought down. I desire, with the permission of the House, to add to this motion these words:-
4.	The names of the shareholders of the present tenant or proprietor company, with the number of shares held by each and the par value of such shares.

Mr. Speaker, before the hon. Minister of Public Works answers my hon. friend with reference to the production of the documents for which he has moved, let me say that the granting of the lease to Mr. Robert of the water-power on the site of the old Beau-harnois canal was the result of a longstanding fight between the citizens of Montreal and the Montreal Light, Heat- and Power Co. For many years, as my hon. friend is aware, the taxpayers of the city of Montreal were endeavouring to get rid of that monopoly. Five or six years ago I took a persona] interest in this matter, along with some citizens of Montreal, and I am glad to say that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was one of those citizens. We were taxpayers of Montreal, and we intended, as soon as possiDie, to get rid of that monopoly.
I am afraid my hon. friend is giving me a merit to which I am not entitled. I have no recollection of this.

I will refresh my hon. friend's memory. Deputations were organized, not to go before the city council, because it was recognized that the citizens of Montreal could not get justice from the city council, but it was realized that there was a magnificent water-power to be had at the Beauharnois canal, which was not being used, and delegations were organized to ask the government at Ottawa to protect the taxpayers of Montreal as against the monopoly known as the Montreal Light, Heat and Power 'Co. I remember the last delegation which came to Ottawa, composed cf some members of the city council of Montreal, including the mayor and my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Mr. Martin), and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
The hon. gentleman is mistaken there.	.
I am sorry to say that my hon. friend has in this instance a bad memory.
I cannot lay claim to such patriotism.

Of course his presence there was all to his credit. He was present at the office of the Prime Minister with the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Mr. Martin), some of the aldermen of Montreal, as well as delegations from the surrounding districts of Jacques Cartier, Laprairie, Beauharnois and the various electoral divisions of Montreal. They all urged, irrespective of politics, that the water-power of the Beauharnois canal should be leased to a strong firm which would not be bought or would not be induced to give up its rights to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company. And this is the reason why it was stipulated there and then and published throughout the press that the government would not call for tenders, but would be given to a body of men, respectable and responsible, the management of the Beauharnois canal water-power. If tenders had been called for, of course the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company would have repeated the very unsavoury operation which took place with regard to the Soulanges, Heron Island and Richelieu river water-powerS. Therefore, when a company came before the Prime Minister, with a subscribed capital of $4,000,000, representing the best elements in the city, the government wisely decided	to lease to it the
Beauharnois canal power. What was the consequence? I happen to know the facts, because I took some part in the fight which took place a year or two ago in Montreal in order to obtain a pure civic administration there. The result was that after that waterpower was given the Canadian Light and Heat Company, the prices for electric energy in Montreal for lighting and heating purposes fell some 30 per cent.
Not quite so much.
To what extent did it fall?
I cannot say, but not so much as that.

Of course I cannot give the exact percentage, but there was a very large reduction, and the people of Montreal to-day are free from the thraldom under which they formerly surrered as regards electrical energy.
We are told that we have given away a very valuable concession for years and years to come. Well, the papers have all been laid before the House. The lease is renewable every twenty-one years during a period of some 70 or 80 years. I happen to know a little about this matter because some year and a half or two years ago, the Prime Minister being ill, I was asked to replace him when the first sod was turned at Beauharnois and the new building was being put up. Let me tell you that the new company have spent some $2,000,000 on this

project. I do not know if my hop. friend has seen the building being erected at St. Timothee, but certainly it will be one of the finest power buildings ever put up on this continent. Ig it reasonable then that a company which has broken the worst monopoly the citizens of Montreal had ever contended against and which is spending so much money should be called on to renew its lease every year. Every one will understand that what was done has been done in the interests of the taxpayers of the city of Montreal.
Is there any clause providing that the company may not amalgamate with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company?
There is.

I think my hon. friend will find that such a clause is in the contract, and it was inserted at the request of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and myself. The Minister of Justice himself (Sir Allen Aylesworth) inserted that clause in order to prevent, the possibility of that company joining the monopoly which had crushed the citizens of Montreal for fifteen years before. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk)-[DOT] and I say it to his credit-joined his efforts with ours. There was no political bias, it was purely a municipal question, and both Conservatives and Liberals joined hands to get rid of the monopoly then existing.
The hon. minister says that the lease is for 70 years renewable every 21 years. When renewable in 21 years, does that mean revising the rates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The contract was brought down three or four days ago and is on the table now.

Just one word in answer to the statement of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that the government had no report before them by engineers on the value of the canal. Before the Soulanges canal was constructed the Beauharnois canal was used for the purposes of navigation. At the time the Conservative government had under consideration the construction of the Soulanges canal, the people along the Beauharnois were very anxious that instead of constructing the Soulanges, the Beauharnois canal should be deepened. But the report of the engineer-no doubt a very distinguished man in his profession-then was that it would be impossible to deepen the Beauharnois canal because along by Val-leyfield there was but a continuation of rock. Now we all know that the Soulanges canal has not been the success which the engineer expected; and the lessees of the Mr. LEMIEUX.
Beauharnois canal discovered that the report of the engineer at that time was altogether wrong because they have succeeded in deepening that canal to the extent of about twelve feet. The people along the Beauharnois take an altogether different view from that taken by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). At the time there was an agitation for the leasing of this canal and I was upon the delegation of which the Hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) has just spoken, which went to Ottawa, not for the purpose of urging the government to refuse to lease this canal but for the purpose of urging it to grant a lease to the present lessees and thus prevent it getting into the hands of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company and in this way deprive the people of Valleyfield, Montreal and the surrounding districts of the cheap electrical power which they so much desired. The Canadian Power Company have expended a sum almost equal to the cost of the canal and are not yet in operation, but the result of their operations has been that the people of Valleyfield are now offered their light and heat at a reduction of 40 per cent. That is one reason why they take an altogether different view from that taken by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier? I have not the lease before me, but my recollection is that it contains a clause which compels that company to give light and power to the city of Valleyfield, to the city of Montreal, to Beauharnois and the surrounding section at prices to be fixed by the Railway Commission. There could be nothing fairer than that. And I submit to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that the conservation of natural resources does not mean locking up those resources but giving them to people with capital who will develop them. We who live on the south side of the St. Lawrence, along the Beauharnois canal, are very well satisfied with this lease. The people generally thought, in view of the report that engineer Munro had made twenty years ago, that the lessees of the Beauharnois canal had been buncoed by the government and were paying prices in advance of what their leases were worth. It remains to be proved whether that company will make the big lot of money that my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) imagines they will.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the House will allow me, I hope, to add a few words to what has been said on the question. As a Montreal city councillor and as a representative of St. Mary's division, I have had the honour to accompany the delegation which, a few years ago, interviewed the ministers with the object of obtaining the lease of the Beauharnois canal on behalf of the Robert Company, as stated

by the hon. Postmaster General a moment ago.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier remembers no doubt that for some time past there was a movement going on in the Montreal city council with a view to effecting a change in the lighting system. We were intent on getting rid of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, which, as stated by the hon. Postmaster General, had full control of the lighting.
Now, the city council, last year, advertised for tenders. The Robert Company put in a tender, and I remember fully well that one evening council sat until midnight in the hope of securing the contract for lighting to that company. However, the majority in the council made all kind of objections, so much so that the company found it impossible to accept the terms set down.
I remember, among other things, that they would not give them a contract for more than five years, and finally, they had to refuse it.
I sincerely believe that the government, by giving a lease to the Robert Company acted in the best interest of the public. It had the result of relieving the people of Montreal, in view of the fact that the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company had to reduce their rates to a very great extent. As a matter of fact, the Montreal Light, till last year, made an allowance of 15 p.c. upon the consumer paying within ten days. It is quite different now. I know what I am talking about, having had a contract with the same company for the lighting of my own house for a period of five years, and I got a discount of 46 p.c.
My opinion is that, while the government may not realize any profit by its lease to Mr. Robert, the benefit will all go to the people living alongside the canal, and more particularly the people of Montreal.
I do not see wThv the member for Jacques Cartier should ask any explanation about this matter. I am sure that the consumers in Montreal will greatly benefit by that arrangement:
I endorse all the statements made by the hon. Postmaster General, and I think that the member for Jacques Cartier ought to be quite satisfied.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
After the remarks which have been made by the hon. gentleman who followed my hon. friend from Jacq,ues Cartier (Mr. Monk), there remains but very little for me to say, beyond giving to the House a summary of the lease which was entered into between His Majesty and Mr. McIntyre and Mr. Robert, of the right to use water of the Beauharnois canal. I think it desirable that the terms of the lease should be placed on * Hansard ' in consequence more especially of the statement of the hon. member from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that he trusted no such lease as this would ever again be entered into by the government. I understand that the reason my hon. friend made that statement is, that he is of the opinion that it does not follow out the principle of conserving the water-powers of the country. My own idea is that the proper way to conserve the water-powers of this country is not to lock them up, not to prevent them from being developed, but to encourage their development and to ensure, as far as it can possibly be done, that power shall be supplied to the people at the lowest possible price. It seems to me that in order to do that, first of all it is desirable that strong men, men of good financial standing, shall be induced to take hold of those water-powers with a view to developing them, that is, unless the government itself, on behalf of the country, is prepared to engage in the development of water-powers as a public work. That has not so far, been done in Canada. It is true that in Ontario they have organized the Hydro-Electric Commission, but that is only a commission for the distribution of water-power, it is not a commission that, so far, has had anything to do with the development of water-powers. The commission purchases its water-power from piivate companies which have expended large sums in the development of power. It seems to me that these are two essentials, but the most important of all is, of course, that this great public utility shall be furnished to the people desirous of using it at the lowest possible cost. In order that the people may get electricity at the lowest possible cost, there must be some permanency of tenure to the company developing the power. If the views of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), should prevail that a company should only be allowed a lease of a water-power for a short period of time, and the lease should then terminate, and if it is my hon. friend's views that the company then should receive no compensation for the money expended in the development of power, which might amount in many cases to a very large sum of money, then in order to recoup themselves, the company would be obliged during the short period of their tenure, to charge very much higher prices for the use of electricity than would otherwise be the case. I do not think that would be desirable or in the interest of the country.
Another feature which I think is essential is, that it should be provided that, if at any time in the future -the government

ox the country should feel it desirable in the public interest to acquire the property and operate it as a public work, the government should be enabled to take over the property of the company on giving fair compensation, which I assume would embrace not only the actual cost, but a reasonable percentage on the moneys the company had invested in its undertaking. It seems to me that in that way, the public interest would be conserved, the people would get electricity at the lowest possible cost and the government would be enabled at any time in the future to take control of the property when it might become necessary to do so in the public interest.
You will agree with me when I have read this lease, that it fulfils every condition which I have suggested to the House as being desirable in the public interest. And looking back now to the time when this lease was executed and 'bearing in mind that the idea of the conservation of water-powers and other natural resources had not advanced to the stage it has now reached, it is remarkable that the government should have exercised such great care iu seeing that in every respect the public interest was guarded in the lease of this water-power. I can account for it by this fact that even before the great number of people who are to-day interested in the conservation of the natural resources of the country became so interested, I can well remember my hon. friend the Prime Minister, both in Ottawa and elsewhere, putting forward in the very strongest manner possible, the desirability of talcing steps for the conservation of the natural resources of our country and to him is largely due the forward movement which conservation has taken during the last few years and the very forward state which it has reached to-day.
The lease was made on December 10, 1907. It is between His Majesty, the King and Mr. William Cassels McIntyre and Mr. Edmund Arthur Robert, both of the city of Montreal. It recites that the Beauharnois canal is no longer needed for purposes of navigation and that it is considered desirable to lease it for the development of electricity for heating, lighting and industrial purposes and for the reasons which are set forth in the order in council, and which are to be found set forth to a considerable degree also in the lease, it was decided to grant a lease without competition to the gentlemen whom I have named. Then it provides that the lessees may have the right to take water from the Beauharnois canal and certain rights are given in the land bordering on the canal. The lease is for a period of 21 years renewable as therein provided, returning therefore the annual rent or sum of $12,000.
For how long may it be renewed ?

There may be two renewals. The lease is for 21 years with two renewals of 21 years each. '
It provides that the lessees shall make all urgent and necessary repairs to the canal and the works in connection therewith subject always to the supervision and approval of the minister. It also provides that the lessees shall at their own cost and expense maintain, perform, operate and keep in good and sufficient repair, all bridges, including farm bridges, ferries, weirs, roads, fences, ditches and culverts, and all other servitudes whatever, which it is now incumbent on His Majesty to maintain and to keep in repair in The premises.
Thus the government is relieved of considerable burdens which would otherwise exist in respeet to bridges crossing the canal and other matters to which this clause refers.
It is also provided that the lessees shall indemnify His Majesty against all liabilities for damage, detriment or injury that may result from the construction, or operation of the works or from neglect to maintain them in an efficient condition. It provides for the rights of the Montreal Cotton Company and of all other lessees. Here is a very important clause:
The lessees shall, whenever so required by the municipality of Valleyfield, or by the municipality of Beauharnois, or other municipality adjacent to the canal, or by the city of Montreal, furnish the municipality or the city with electrical power for municipal lighting purposes at reasonable rates and on reasonable conditions, such rates and conditions in the event of disagreement between the parties to be determined by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada; provided always that notification of such requirements be given by the municipalities respectively, or the city, as the case may be, to the lessees within two years from the grant of this lease, and that reasonable time be allowed the lessees after such notification to enable them to comply therewith.
You will see that evidently one of the objects which the government had in view was to enable the municipalities of Valley-field, Beauharnois, and any other municipality adjacent to the canal, as well as the city of Montreal, to secure electrical power for municipal lighting purposes at reasonable rates, and it is provided that if the company and these municipalities cannot agree upon the rates, then they are to be fixed by the Board of Railway Commissioners. That. I think, Mr. Speaker, is a very important safeguard for the public interest. Then, certain other provisions are made with regard to sewer pipes, carrying cables over the canal, &e.

My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier stated that there is no provision that there shall be an increase of rental in case the company should develop additional power. Well, as I said before, I do not think the matter of increasing the revenue of the country is of such great importance as the reduction of the cost of lighting and power. It is the reduction of the cost of the supply of these important utilities to the people that is the essential thing to be aimed at, but, even in the suggestion which my hon. friend made that there is no power to increase the rental, I think it will be found that he is entirely wrong because my hon. friend would agree with me that it would not be possible, at all events, not reasonably possible-indeed, I do not think possible at all-to increase the power unless the flow of water through the Beauharnois canal were increased. That would necessitate the deepening and widening of the Beauharnois canal, so as to give a larger intake and to allow more water to flow into the canal. It is expressly provided by the lea^e that no work of that kind shall be undertaken except with the approval of the minister, who must be satisfied that any such works will in no way interfere with the level of the St. Lawrence river, and as no such works can be undertaken except with the consent of the minister, it would be quite within his power, if he thought it in the public interest, to exact a larger rental commensurate with the additional power which would be derived by the company by reason of the enlargement of the intake and the consequent increase in the flow of water.
I would like to ask the minister if any such additional works have been undertaken.
No, not as yet, but plans for such works are now before the government, and are under the consideration of the engineers.
They have not yet been approved?
Is there not a clause in the lease that the rates shall be under the control of the Governor General in Council?

Yes, I read that. They are under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. In so far as the rates are concerned, my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) spoke of there being a revision of the rental. That is of some importance from the financial standpoint in so far as the country at large is concerned. It might very well be, that, as the water-powers of this kind belong to the nation, the nation should receive a certain rental-not an un-

reasonable rental, but a fair, reasonable rental for the use of these water-powers- but what is of far greater importance than the question of rental is the question of the rates which the people are to pay for the use of electricity, light and power, and this lease expressly provides that every five years the rates that the company can charge these municipalities may be revised by the Board of Railway Commissioners. This is a most important provision and I think it is evidence of the very great care which the government exercised in the preparation of this lease. Then, Sir, I come to another provision, which I think is also of vast importance, and it is this:
If the demised premises or any portion thereof shall be required for public purposes, possession of the same may at any time during the said term be resumed by the government upon twelve months' notice in writing by the minister to the lessees. Upon such resumption all privileges and rights of the lessees hereunder shall cease, arid His Majesty shall pay to the lessees the value, with an addition of five per cent thereon, 'of all work, plant, buildings, machinery and material done, erected, built, or placed by the lessees under this lease in or upon the leased premises or upon other premises leased or required by them, for the purpose of converting the hydraulic power of the canal into electric power and of disposing of the same in Beau-harnois, Valley field, or other municipality adjacent to the canal or in Montreal, including the transmission and distribution system, such value to be fixed by arbitration as hereinafter provided as representing the fair value of the same in the then existing conditions.
To summarize briefly the important provisions of this lease-we have the fact that a fixed rental is reserved, that no works can be undertaken for the enlargement of the intake and thus increasing the flow of water and consequently the power, without the consent of the minister who can impose such terms as he thinks best in the public interest. We have the fact also that no assignment can take place without the assent of the minister, and upon assignment being made the controlling interest dn the capital stock must be placed in a trust company. Then 51 per cent of the capital stock is placed in the Montreal Trust Company, by the agreement entered into, >a copy of which is attached to the lease, for the purpose of ensuring that amalgamation should not take place between the company and the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company. We have the further provision that the charges for light and power to these municipalities adjacent to the canal and to the city of Montreal, shall be subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and subject to revision every five years. W'e have also the further and important provision, that the government, whenever it may deem it Mr. PUGSLEY.
advisable in the public interest to do so, may take over all the rights of the lessees, all their power, all their plant, all their works of development, all their transmission lines, on simply paying the actual value to the company with an advance of five per cent thereon. It seems to me that if the hon. member for Jacques Cartier were to set to work to prepare a lease that would most effectually carry out the best ideas of those interested in conserving the water-powers of the country it would be impossible for him to improve upon the lease which the government gave in respect to the power in the Beauharnois canal. There is no objection, of course, to giving the information asked for in the notice as printed, but the hon. gentleman has amended the motion to ask that the government shall lay upon the table of the House a list of the shareholders in this company. There is no such list of shareholders so far as I am aware in any of the departments of the government. There is no provision in the charter by which a list of the shareholders is to be submitted to the government, and it would, therefore, be impossible for the government to comply with the motion if it were amended as asked by the hon. member.

After the description given by the Minister of Public Works of the absolute control and power which the government have over the grantees of the Beauharnois canal, I am surprised that he should find it impossible to consent to the proposed amendment by which it is sought to obtain a list, of the shareholders, and the par value of the shares of this company. Surely if the government has all this influence over this company it is possible for the minister to obtain for parliament a list of the shareholders, particularly in view of a stipulation that a proportion of the shares will be placed in the hands of a trust company in the event of a transfer by the original grantees. It is very important under the circumstances that we should know Who are the partied interested in this company and in the grant, and unless the House is adverse to getting that information I shall insist upon that part of the motion. It seems somewhat strange that just at this moment when the discussion of the disposition of our national wealth is so prominent, that a demand for such information as I have asked should be met with so much protest. I presume the Postmaster General is speaking as acting Minister of Railways, and if one were to believe him the whole of this transaction was dictated to the government by a zealous desire to come to the assistance of the city of Montreal which he says was some years ago suffering from the oppression of a powerful

company which distributes electricity throughout the city. Therefore, according to the Postmaster General, in order to come to the assistance of the city of Montreal, the government without observing the rules and principles which now obtain throughout the civilized world in regard to *such matters, conceded this power upon most favourable and happy terms to Mr. McIntyre and the other gentlemen associated with him. I wonder if it occurred at that time to the Postmaster General, that it would have been a fit and proper thing- as the establishment of a municipal lighting plant for the city of Montreal was then being discussed, and is to-day a live question-to offer these singular advantages to the city of Montreal itself. Why was not that done? Why was not such an offer made? It will be difficult to understand why it was absolutely necessary, in order to relieve the situation in the city of Montreal, to concede such a very favourable grant to two gentlemen, who, if we are well informed, have since, upon the transfer of that grant realized very considerable profits. That is a question of some importance. Was the situation of the city of Montreal at that date so bad that it was necessary in conceding this grant to omit all the precautions which generally surround grants of that nature. Why was not a careful survey made of the Beauharnois canal, and an estimate prepared by experts, setting out upon what terms that grant should be made, what the rental, and what conditions should be attached to it. None of these formalities, judging by what we have heard from the treasury benches this afternoon, were observed at that time. The Minister of Public Works tells us that the grant is not perpetual. Well, until we have carefully examined the deed it is difficult to see how far it extends, and what length of time it gives to the grantees or their assigns, but the minister himself has told us that it was a grant for 63 or 64 years. At Quebec, during the discussion of this most important subject, very strong objection was made to a grant over 50 years, and it was stated there by competent persons that a grant for that length of time was absolutely contrary to the public interest. I myself did not share that view, and I urged at the time that it was impossible within a period of 20 or 25 years in the case of important concessions given to concessionnaries to have sufficient time to carry out the scheme of development. But, 64 years is a very long period indeed, particularly as I assume from what has been stated by the minister that the rental continues the same during the whole period of the lease. The state receives upon a capital expenditure of over two million dollars, a revenue of $12,000 per year, which does not vary. It
is true, as the minister says, that improvements and changes cannot be made without the consent of the government. But nowhere in that clause did I hear my hon. friend point out that if improvements and changes were made which the government could not otherwise accept, it might avail itself of that opportunity to exact additional rental. That would not be honest or proper on the part of the government, under the clause read by my hon. friend. It was not contemplated that improvements and changes would give rise to an increase of rental. It is now well known to everybody that a clause such as that mentioned by my hon. friend will not prevent a merger of interests, an evasion of what was contemplated by the clause, a fusion between these grantees or their assigns and the company mentioned by my hon. friend. There are so many devices known to the public by which clauses of that kind may be entirely set at nought that it seems almost a childish argument in the mouth of my hon. friend to suggest that such an obstacle could not be overcome. For instance, suppose this company made a contract to furnish electricity, not to the city of Montreal, but to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company-my hon. friend is a lawyer-would we have a right to intervene? No. Our right to intervene, and the application of the clause cited by my hon. friend, is restricted to the case of the grantees or their assigns undertaking to furnish electricity to the city of Montreal. It is, therefore, open to this company-and this is only one way out of many-under this very deed, to furnish electricity to those who furnish electricity to the city of Montreal, without in any way coming under the control of the clause invoked by my hon. friend. My hon. friend the Postmaster General seemed to claim great merit for having brought about a diminution of rates in the city of Montreal.

Not personally. I said the citizens who led the movement for better treatment on the part of the electric company. I claimed credit, not for myself, but in company with my hon. friend and the delegation which came to Ottawa at that time to ask for that power.

I would be glad to give credit to my hon. friend for the great public spirit which he manifested at that time and since, but I do not think the facts are exactly as he says. This company has not yet reached Montreal; it is not furnishing electricity there, and, although I would not utter a single word in disparagement of the great company which my hon. friend the Postmaster General thinks so poorly of, I do not think they are of a disposition to be terrified by what is going on now at the Beauharnois canal, for they long before-

hand began reducing their rates to their customers. I quite sided with those who thought we were paying excessive rates, because it seemed to me that the city of Montreal, surrounded on all sides with water-powers of great magnitude, easily developed, ought to have electricity just as cheap, even much cheaper, than the city of Toronto, for instance. But other companies have since established themselves at Montreal, and this is the real cause of the reduction of rates.

My hon. friend will admit that the first break in the monopoly was the granting of that lease of the Beau-harnois canal, and since that policy was adopted there has been a reversal of public opinion in Montreal. Last year the good municipal organization fought a battle which brought victory, and since that victory the Local League of Quebec has given all other electric companies the power to operate in Montreal, and a commission was granted by the Quebec government, as a result of the fight which was begun here in the Prime Minister's office, where my hon. friend was so conspicuous in his advocacy of improvements which would bring about cheaper electricity.
ONIi. I do not know whether my hon. friend refers to the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Mr. Martin).

The hon. member for St. Mary's division was taken to task last year, and the new city council accorded an investigation of the charges against him, but no one would bring a charge against him, and the worst opponents he had with regard to his municipal career had to admit that there was nothing against him.

I will not dispute my hon. friend's statement, When my hon. friend refers to the good municipal government which ws have in Montreal, I quite agree with him that we had an end put to a state of affairs which was almost intolerable, but the result of the popular vote on that occasion does not seem to have favoured my hon. friend from St. Mary's division, and I would assume, from what he said to-day, that his electors were very ungrateful to him, after all he had done to reduce the price of electricity. Now, Sir, I have spoken of the futility of the clause mentioned by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. As a matter of fact-and this is some justification, I hope, for my asking for these documents-at the present moment there is a rumour of an arrangement practically amounting to a merger,"or amalgamation between the very grantees to whom this concession was made and this very company which has been so much animadverted upon to-day by my hon. friends opposite. The grant was made some Mr. MONK.
time ago. Transfers have taken place since, the government has intervened, payments have been made, at the present moment communications are passing between the government and this new company, and I hope we shall have all these documents before the House, as we are entitled to see them. To the control of rates under these circumstances I would apply the same argument as I would apply to the argument made by the Minister of Public Works respecting the furnishing of electricity to the city of Montreal. The right to control the rates arises when this company furbishes electricity to the city of Montreal. Until then there is no such right. Does it arise if the grantees or their assigns furnish electricity to the. Light, Heat and Power Company? It does not seem so, from the clause read here by the hon. minister. Besides, we know what this control of rates amounts to nowadays. Companies must be allowed to collect sufficient revenue to pay the interest upon their capital and debentures, and we know something of watered stock, of over-capitalized companies, to know of what worth such an argument is in the mouths of those who carry out transactions of that kind. It is better to foresee than, to apply a remedy, which, under the circumstances, must necessarily be nugatory one-half the time, if not more.
I ask the hon. member to let me say one word in order to answer the insinuation that he has made a moment ago against me.
When I shall have done you will speak as you like.
When you shall have done it will be impossible for me to speak because, according to the rules of the House the discussion shall be closed and nobody can speak after you.

I said that there were other companies in the city of Montreal. We have the Saraguay Company, we have the Central Light and Heating Company, there are other companies projected, there is the possibility of the city of Montreal establishing a lighting and heating plant itself, and there is, as my hon. friend the

Postmaster General stated, the new administration of the city of Montreal. These facts, and these alone, have influenced the movement to which my ihon. friend the Postmaster General pointed a moment ago.
I find that there is no change in the rental. I find that the alienation is for more than half a century; ipossible it may be more than that; but, according to my hon. friend, it provides for sixty-three or sixty-four years of enjoyment, and I do not find that the clause invoked by my hon. friend as amply protecting the city of Montreal, is sufficient excuse for the government having violated in this instance the cardinal principles of alienation as they are recognized by all the authorities on the subject, short periods of alienation, changes of rates according to the amount of power developed, absolute control of rates under all circumstances, and, above all, the tender of an opportunity to all the citizens of Canada to make an offer before an alienation takes place.'
^ If the House will allow me, I would like to* answer the insinuation which has been made about me a moment ago by the honourable member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
I cannot allow the hon. member to go on with his speech, the debate being closed, and he having already addressed the House on the subject.	.

I wish to speak on a question of privilege, with a view to giving some personal explanations.
While it is true that last year an investigation was carried on under a Royal Commission into the affairs of the Montreal city council, that investigation was held at my own request.
Without going into the particulars, I may say at the outset that having taken an aggressive stand in regard to the city council, having branded my eollegues as ' boodlers ' and tliiefs, it was natural that they should do all in their power to crush me by -whatever means available. Things even went to the point that false affidavits were forged, but the commissioner conducting the inquiry would not allow me to defend myself. Nevertheless, I was one of the eight who were singled out in the commissioner's report. I called on the Montreal city council at the time to institute proceedings against me, in order to give me a chance to vindicate myself, but without avail. I requested the present council to institute proceedings against me, in order to give me an opportunity of defending myself, but the new council did not move any more than their predecessors. I even went a step further, Mr. Speaker, and asked
the attorney general for the province of Quebec to take proceedings against me so that I might be in a position to shoiv the falsity of the charges laid against my character. Here again, I -was unsuccessful.
If the hon. member for Jacques -Cartier, who has thought fit to refer here to these slanderous insinuations, is serious, knowing as he does that a man guilty of fraud and corruption in the way that he gave the House to understand that I had been, that such a man, I say, ;s unworthy of occupying a seat in this House, it is incumbent on him- and I challenge him to do so-to move for an investigation into my dealings, in order to find out wThetner or not I was guilty of -such offences, whether or not there is any foundation to these charges against me. Let him move for an inquiry whereby my right to occupy a seat in this House "will be settled one way or another. If I am unworthy of occupying a seat in this House, that inquiry will show it. It is the only means of finding out the truth in this connection and of vindicating my good name. I would welcome such a move on the part of the member of Jacques Cartier, as it would put me in a position of defending myself and setting matters right.
Notwithstanding what Judge Cannon or anybody else may have stated. I challenge whomsoever it may be to show that I failed in doing my duty while sitting m the Montreal city council, and I fear none of the insinuations which may be aimed at me, and especially by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.
I object to any important amendment being added ter the motion.

Objection being taken, I find that, according to Bourinot, the motion must be according to the notice given and its terms cannot be * altered without the consent of the House. I therefore cannot allow any amendment.

REPORT OF THE IMPERIAL DEFENCE CONFERENCE, 1909.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable for the convenience of members of the House and of the public, to provide additional copies of the printed report of the Imperial defence conference of July and August, 1909.
He said: I hope there will be no objection to the expression of this wish. I think the members of the House will admit that the Imperial Defence Conference of 1909 was a very important event indeed in the history of this country; that arrangements were arrived at there the result of which was to change in very large measure the understanding between the British government and the government of this country regarding the defence of this country and the share of Canada in the general defence of the empire. These arrangements and agreements are contained in a blue-book the supply which failed very long ago when we should have had an ample supply of a document of such importance. The consequence is that to-day-and even long before to-day-when any body wishes to refer to the discussions and proceedings of the Imperial Defence Conference of 1909, it is impossible to secure copies. Members of the House know the exceedingly large quantity of blue-books printed, to my mind unnecessarily, when you consider the matters treated in many of them. We are embarrass-Mr. MONK.
ed from one year's end to the other with printed matter of which a very limited supply would, I think, suffice concerning analysis of honey or fertilizers or other such matters. But this imperial defence conference report is a document to which reference requires to be made continually, which the public desire to consult, which we wish to have at hand, and which will be required for a long time to come. Last year, before the session was half over, it was very difficult to obtain any copies of this blue-book. I myself suffered much inconvenience in this regard. One applied for the blue-book and could not get it; the French version particularly was wanting in an extraordinary degree. And during the public discussion and public meetings which followed the session during the by-election we could not possibly obtain a copy of this important document which the whole discussion bore upon. I have laid upon the table the letters of the three officers of the House from whom we most naturally would expect readily to obtain copies of the English and French versions of this report, but By these letters it will appear that I could get neither, because, as was stated, the supply was exhausted. i\Ve will require these documents again, and it is convenient that we should have them handy. This is not a very voluminous document; and I hope the House will adopt the expression of this desire that we should have easy access to this document, and that a certain number be printed in both languages.
While on my feet, I would like to say that I have been informed on very creditable authority that the whole verbatim report of that conference had been transmitted to Canada, and that certain members of the House had that word for word report what was said at the conference as well as of what was decided and done. That is what happened with regard to previous conferences. What I wish to call particular attention to is that some members of the House have access to that verbatim report though it was refused to others, and these others had no opportunity of seeing it. If this motion is carried, I hope the government will carry out the suggestion I make that the whole report be printed and placed at the disposal of members of the House.

There is certainly no objection to the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) being carried. I understand that he refers to the blue-book brought down to the House last session. If there were no more copies printed, it is certainly not the fault of the government. I understand that questions relating to the printing of blue-books are decided by the joint committee on printing, a committee composed of members, of the Senate and members of the House of Commons. This com-

mittee has standing rules stating how many copies of each blue-book have been printed and distributed, and, unless they pass some orders to 'the contrary, this standing Tule would apply. I understand that the rule has been covered in this case. But I see that the number of copies of the French edition especially-I do not know anything about the English-are exhausted. Under these circumstances, there is no objection- quite the contrary-on the part of the government that some more copies should be printed. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) however, does not state in his motion what would be the number of copies required. Perhaps it would be better to have this defined in the resolution, in order that the clerk of the House may immediately give the necessary instructions for printing, or, what will be still more regular, refer the matter to the joint committee on printing to determine the additional number of copies required. But, as to the principle of the motion, there is absolutely no objection.

speechtext: I should like to second the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that the full report of the proceedings should be printed. I suppose that the government has that report. I presume the government could obtain the consent of the home government to have the report printed for parliament. I see no reason why we should not have not only the conclusions which were arrived at, but what is far more important, the grounds which were urged for or against those conclusions, and the attitude on these various questions of the representatives of the other Dominions of the empire. In the case of the conference of 1902, I think the Prime Minister himself suggested that there was no reason why the report should not be published in full and if I remember correctly he said he would communicate with the home government.

He said: I mentioned this to the Prime Minister the other day. The facts are that a preventive officer in the county of Halifax holding a position which commands a salary of $150 a year happened to be elected in November or December as member of the municipal council of the county of Halifax. After his election it was brought to his attention that his position as a preventive officer might be lost by holding the position of municipal councillor. He wrote to me to ascertain whether this intimation '

was correct. I made application to the Department of Customs and in reply received from them the following regulation:

Department of Customs, Canada, Ottawa, 2nd January, 1906. To Collectors of Customs:

The attention of customs officers is directed to the following regulation, under order of the Governor General in Council:-
' No officer of customs is allowed to hold any corporate office, nor to interfere in political questions, either local or general.'
That portion seems to be the language of the order in council. Then the memorandum continues:-
The corporate offices above referred to are such offices as warden, mayor, alderman, school trustee, councillor, &c.
The rule applies to officers in the inside and outside service of the Customs.

Commissioner of Customs.
As I understand it, no copy of this memorandum was ever sent to the officer to whom I allude. It is perfectly clear that the salary of $150 a year which he enjoys is absolutely insufficient for the support of himself and his family. It is, therefore, abundantly evident that a very considerable portion of his time must be devoted, and is devoted, to seeking other means of support. As a matter of fact, his appointment is simply made for the convenience of a small number of vessels visiting this outport, and he does not pretend, nor is it expected by the Department of Customs, that he should devote the whole of his time to the performance of his duties. The office to which he has been elected as a member of the municipal council of the county of Halifax takes, I suppose, ten, or twelve, or possibly fifteen days in each year; that is to say, he wculd be absent from his home at Ingram docks, in the county of Halifax, about that number of days in each year. The unfortunate position of matters at the present time is that his district will remain unrepresented for a portion of the year, because he cannot resign until he is sworn in after the council meets, and there will not be time to elect another representative of the district.
Well, what I desire to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister is, in the first place, that this seems to be a rather paltry and unnecessary rule in so far as officers of that status are concerned. I entirely agree that employees of the government of Canada, even holding a very small position, such as this man, ought not to interfere offensively in political affairs-I mean in federal or provincial elections-but I am bound to say that I see no particular reason Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
why they should not be elected as members .of the municipal councils, which, in this particular instance, and, I think, generally throughout the country, are hot run on federal or provincial political lines. That rule seems to be rather unnecessary in so far as officers of this character are concerned.
mere is no such rule generally prevailing in ail of the departments of government, or else the rule is absolutely violated every day. I am not speaking from personal knowledge, but I am informed on good authority that there are at the present time, in the council of the city of Ottawa, no less than three civil servants who are receiving remuneration of a very considerable character and the whole of whose time is supposed to be devoted to the public service. Now, why is it that a civil servant at Ottawa, receiving a salary of $1,500 or $2,000, is at liberty to become a member of the city council and participate in the municipal government of this city and an officer holding the petty position to which I have alluded, a position commanding a salary of $150, and taking only a few days of his time in each year, should be debarred from doing exactly the same thing? It is perfectly obvious that the rules of the different departments are not the same, or that these rules are not being carried out. Therefore,
I have asked for a return, which will set forth a copy of the orders in council, regulations, rules, &c., touching upon thi3 subject. I think it is desirable that we should have some statement of the principle or policy upon which the government is acting in such matters, and that we should also know exactly what any employee of the government throughout the country serving in any department is to expect. So far as the unfortunate individual whose case I have brought to the attention of the House is concerned, he entered into this election contest in absolute ignorance of any rule or regulation which would debar him from doing so, and as a result he, and the district which he represents, have been placed in the unfortunate position which I have pointed out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker.
I confess that I was somewhat taken by surprise when my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Borden, Halifax) informed the House that this customs officer in Halifax, who receives a salary, if salary it can be called, of $150 a year, should be called upon at the same time to resign a position to which he had been elected in the municipal service of his district. It is evident that this officer cannot liye on the salary that he receives, that he must have another mode of living, that this is only an adjunct to his ordinary avocation, that, therefore, he is more of a private citizen than an official of the government, and I must say that under such

circumstances I could not see the reason of the rule which has been exercised against him. But, I have not been able yet to take the matter up, as my colleague the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) is away, but I intend, on his return, to confer with him and have the reason for such a'rule, if such a rule exists.
At the same time, I must express my satisfaction with my hon. friend that he has brought the matter to the attention of the House, because evidently there is an anomaly which must be rectified in what is going on. It is perfectly true that at this moment there are three members of the civil service who are now in the service of ' the city of Ottawa. One or two of them are aldermen, and one is on the board of control. No exception has been taken to their election, and though some of them were elected after a somewhat severe contest, I am not aware-it has not reached me-that any exception has been taken by anybody to these particular candidates because they were in the service. On the other hand, I have at this moment correspondence showing that in another city where men similarly situated, that is, being in the service of the government, attempted to be candidates, objection was immediately taken to them. It is very often found here and elsewhere, that there are men in the service who enjoy the confidence of the community in which they live to the extent that no one has found fault with them when they sought to take part in the municipal politics of their locality. In other localities men quite respectable, but still having their enemies, as most of us have, were confronted with notice of objection the moment they attempted to enter municipal politics. Under such circumstances, I believe that we shall have to adopt a uniform rule. I have not talked over the matter, and I would be obliged for any opinion that would come from the other side of the House, but, expressing my own opinion, I would say that, perhaps, the safest course would be to make the rule absolutely uniform that any man in the service of the government obtaining a salary which provides for his living-I do not mean a customs officer who is receiving only $150 a year-should be debarred from entering the municipal service. I would not call on any man who is now in possession of a municipal office to resign, and, perhaps, the best course would be to give notice that in future no man who is a servant of the government should be allowed to enter the municipal council of the locality in which he lives. Either, the rule must be that all servants of the government shall be allowed to enter municipal politics or else that all shall be debarred from so doing. I do not think the present practice of allowing some employees of the government to enter municipal politics and others not, should be allowed to continue.

I would suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is going to make a rule of that kind he should only apply it to civil servants who are in receipt of large salaries and who are supposed to devote all their time to the service of the government. All good citizens owe a duty to the municipality in which they live, and the civil servants owe that duty as well as the rest of tire community. I think the government of this great country should be willing to put themselves to some little inconvenience, if some valued citizen who happens to be in the employ of the government, should be selected by his fellow citizens to represent them in the civic administration. If any salary limit is made, I would suggest that only those who receive large salaries should be debarred from accepting municipal honours.

When I was Minister of Railways we had a great deal of difficulty in the department with reference to this very matter. We must recognize that the municipalities pay practically nothing for the services of their representatives. For example, in the city of Moncton, the remuneration is so paltry, if it is anything at all, that it could not strike any one to engage in civic politics, but there were cases in which men who sought the suffrage of the people, were foremen in different" departments of the railway, and it was represented that as they had, in consequence of their position, control over the voters, it was unfair to those who were running against them. One hon. member has stated that these municipal contests are not run on party lines, but I think it is the experience of every hon. gentleman here that it is an unfortunate fact that too often party politics do enter into municipal contests. There should be discrimination as to what officers should be allowed to seek municipal honours, in any general rule that may be established, and when I was Minister of Railways that principle was given effect to.
What was the principle; I do pot understand.

The principle is that where a man in the government service has control of a large number of men under him, and can grant them favours, he should not be allowed to enter into these contests. It is not that the government loses very much of the time of the employees by attending to their municipal office, but there were constant complaint that the government official had an advantage over the other man who was opposing him.
Mr. McGlVERIN. (Ottawa). It is very probable that this question concerns more

particularly the city of Ottawa than any other municipality in the Dominion. The citizens of Ottawa have had the <rood fortune to have had many memhers^of the Civil Service represent them on the board of aldermen, on the school board, and in seme cases on the board of control. It would seem to me, Sir, that where we have a large body of civil servants, as in this capital city, gentlemen who are paying their taxes and who are deeply interested in the good government of the city, they should be allowed to have the ordinary rights of citizenship and permitted to aspire to any municipal office which is in the gift of their fellow citizens. If there should be any question as to their civic duties interfering with the discharge of the duties of their official position, that can be easily set right, because the deputy minister of any department can see that the official attends to the work of his office. Of course, the first duty of such officials would be to earn the salary they are paid by the government of the country, but surely in their spare hours, after they have rendered full service to the State, they should be entitled to take part in the municipal government of this city. It would appear to me that one of the great difficulties in this country, is to get men of position and intelligence to interest themselves in municipal affairs, and if we are to make a rule that no civil servant shall enter municipal politics, then the city of Ottawa would be deprived of some of its most honoured municipal representatives. We have been fortunate in Ottawa that we have had some very good men, particularly members of the Civil Service, to represent us in the city council, and on the board of control and on the school board. In this city the government officials, do not, as a rule, come under that class referred to by the member for Westmorland who is in a position to wield an influence over other employees, and consequently, the condition of affairs spoken of by that hon. gentleman, would not be applicable here. For my part, I would be extremely sorry to see any rule adopted by the government which would preclude members of the Civil Service, at all events in the city of Ottawa, representing their fellow citizens in municipal matters.

I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) that those who enter the public service should not be permitted to enter municipal politics. I should think that a civil servant running for municipal office might be able to wield a very unfair influence as against his neighbour who is not in the service. If the matter is dealt with jby the government, and there is to be an exception made of the city of Ottawa I do not think that I would enter very much objection, Mr. McGIVERIN.
but, as a general rule the civil servant cannot do justice to the public interest for which he is paid and at the same time do justice to the municipality. I know of cases where gentlemen of the Civil Service have entered municipal politics very much to the injury of the Civil Service, and I do not know that they were very much use to the municipality. When gentlemen enter the Civil Service, with the advantages it affords, it seems to me that they should devote their time and energy and ability to that service, and if they do that, I do not believe they will do more than justice to the reward they receive.

May I be permitted to explain that if my hon. friend referred to me as having objected to government officials taking ipart in municipal or civic affairs, I failed to make myselif understood. The point I wished to make was this. The rigiht hon. leader of the government intimated that some general rule, perhaps a sweeping rule, would be desirable, and I asked him to discriminate by taking into consideration the relative positions of the officials. I thought it was not a question of the payment which they might receive from the municipality or the city, but a broader principle-that possibly men in the government service should be permitted to give their services to the advantage of the community in 'which they reside.

If I may be permitted, I did understand the remarks of the hon. gentleman in the light in which I spoke. Now I understand that he wants to draw a line, and I would like him to tell us where he would draw that line. If I understood him aright, he would draw it at the employees of a government railway. There are a great many others in the government service, however, whom it would be even more objectionable to have engaged in municipal affairs. Even men in the employ of a great company can wield and do wield an unfair influence in a small community as compared with other men.

I think in the course of ten years L have not had the pleasure of agreeing with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister until now. Listening to the debate, I find that the ideas enunciated by the right hon. gentleman are more in harmony with what I think would be a safe rule than any that have been expressed subsequently. 1 think the only safe way would be that those who earn their livelihood in the Civil Service of the country should be debarred from entering anything in the nature of political life. We cannot shut our eyes to the fact that municipal politics are to some extent diverted into political channels. It

is a happy circumstance when it is not so ; but it is the rule, almost if not wholly universal, that the municipal elections have a bearing upon the subsequent parliamentary elections ; and I think it would be a very dangerous thing-and here I agree with another gentleman whom 1 do not often agree with, the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee)-if the large army of civil servants that we have in Ottawa-and if this government is permitted to remain in power long, the army will increase in number-were allowed to engage in the municipal warfare of the city of Ottawa. An exception might be made in the somewhat limited number of cases of persons who are so locally situated that it is found convenient to employ them to perform some minor office for the government ; but the exception should be confined pretty strictly to that class of cases. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) said he would like to have discrimination, and. that the position of the person aspiring to municipal honours should be the determining factor ; that if he were a person likely to exercise influence over those who voted for him, it would be improper for him to have the position. On the other hand, if it be a position in which he would not likely exercise influence, he might well be allowed to exercise the rights of citizenship. But who is to draw the line? Is the candidate to ask permission of hi3 minister to be allowed to take this position or not? And, if he is, where is the guarantee that all will be treated alike? I confess that I would not have perfect faith that all the employees of the various departments would have equal justice ; and we can well imagine that if a head of a department has to draw the line, there might be a feeling, and might perhaps be justified, that there was unjust discrimination, and that a Conservative, for instance, would be prevented serving a Liberal given that privilege. Or there might be a Conservative and a Liberal opposing each other, so that the minister would have practically the power to determine which one should be in the municipal council and which should not. I trust, therefore, the government will take this matter into early consideration, and make a rule on the lines the Prime Minister has indicated, that those who are drawing comfortable incomes from the Civil Service shall feel obliged to give all their energies to that service and shall not consider it a hardship to be deprived from engaging in municipal affairs.

It seems to me we can hardly apply the same rule to both classes of civil servants, namely, those in Ottawa and those on the Intercolonial railway, because the cases are not at all par-71
allel. In a city like this the rule that I would be disposed to apply would be that when civil servants who own property and are therefore on a par with other citizens, they should have the right to go into municipal life because municipal officers have the power to tax or prevent taxation of property. If civil servants are property owners to an extent sufficient to qualify them for municipal office, I would be inclined to the opinion that they should have the right to be elected to those offices. But I would go a step further. I would make the civil servants here the same as any other citizens. I would enable their creditors to collect debts from them and deal with them in the business relations of life just as they would with other individuals. If that be done, I can see no reason why it would not be perfectly proper for civil servants to accept municipal office and take their share of municipal government the same as other property owners. It is unfortunate that in some parts of the country, of late years there has been a tendency to run these municipal campaigns on political lines. That is very wrong and it sometimes gives a civil servant an advantage in a contest which he should not enjoy. We ought to discredit as much as possible the tendency to run municipal contests on political iines. With that understanding, I can see no objection to civil servants who are property owners being elected to municipal office.
But when we come to the employees of the Intercolonial railway, who have a great deal of business patronage to dispense, the case is different. Take an important employee on the Intercolonial railway in some town where he can control many things, that railway has much to do with the municipality, and in such a case I think that these civil servants should not be eligible for municipal election. I think that there you might probably draw the line and say that where the employee is receiving a reasonable salary, he should give his whole time to the service and not take part in municipal matters.
