But if he be only in receipt of a trifling salary, such as $100 or $150, it ought to be beneath us to make any rule prohibiting such a man from taking part in municipal life, if he be qualified in other respects.

In a former debate I had occasion to express the same opinion as has been giyen to-night by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Bor- * den) and the right hon. the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) with regard to the recipient of such a paltry salary as $150. These parties should not be disqualified from participating in any of the duties of citizenship. However, I find the expression of opinion prevalent in the House that the government does not



begrudge the time which civil servants may bestow on their duties as councillors or municipal officers. If there be no objection on the part of the government to let civil servants give their time to the discharge of such duties, this subject might well be dropped in this House altogether. The qualification of our aldermen or municipal councillors is a purely local matter to be dealt with by the local legislatures. If any one will look over the statutes of the different provinces, he will find many which disqualify certain persons from running for municipal councils, such as sheriffs, clergymen and municipal employees; so that if we do not begrudge the time given to these municipal duties, it is perfectly safe for us to leave to the legislatures of the different provinces the duty of saying who shall be eligible. If any one who is running should abuse the office he holds from the government, that will very soon become lrnown, and it will be in the hands of the local legislature to disqualify any such person. But there is no power in this House to enforce any such regulation except by the drastic method of dismissal. But if a regulation is to be enforced, let it be enforced by the local legislatures. Not so very long ago we had a drastic regulation in force in the province of Nova Scotia which prevented Dominion officials from voting in a Dominion election. I had the honour of introducing a Bill into the legislature of Nova Scotia to remove such disqualifications. So, I think, in the province from which I come, we are advancing along the line of being willing that Dominion officials should take part in municipal government. And, as I said, if this House is willing that the time should be devoted to the service of the municipality, I think we can well leave it to the provincial authorities to decide who are eligible for such positions.

I have listened with great interest to the opinions expressed on this question, and perhaps I may not agree with any of them. I think that as to the inside service here in Ottawa, when a man accepts a public position with a fixed salary, he agrees to give all his time and all his services to the country. It may be said that his hours only extend from 9 a.m. or 9.30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and that outside of that time he is free to do what he pleases. I do not so regard it. I think the civil servant is paid for all his time and for his whole service, and that, besides the time, he spends in his office he should give time to rest and recreation in order to better fit him for his duties. But, if he takes advantage of that, and devotes five or six hours of the evening to a municipal council meeting, he is certainly not going to be as well prepared for service next day, Mr. McKenzie.
and I do not think it fair to the country that he should accept the salary paid to a civil servant, and waste energy, if not his time,'in doing work other than that which the country requires of him.
I think it would be a hardship to impose this condition upon the outside service, upon the man who does not agree to give all his time or, possibly, even more than a small part of his time, to the service' of the country, as in the case instanced by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). It seems to me it would be rather a hardship to deprive such a man of the right to run for municipal office. But he is in a vastly different position from that of a civil servant at Ottawa, who accepts payment for his entire time. I have had occasion, before now, to appeal to the Minister of Customs in a matter somewhat similar, the case of a collector of customs in my own county who was running a hotel. I thought it not a reasonable thing that a man should hold these two positions. However, I think I was overruled. Nevertheless, I contend I was right. I do not think a man engaged in commercial business should be permitted to be an officer of the customs and pass his own goods through the customs. But that is very different from a civil servant engaging in municipal affairs. I think a civil servant whose whole time is paid for by the country should abstain from having anything to do with municipal affairs, but should give his entire time to the service of the country, including the time of rest and recreation which he should use in better preparing himself for his duties.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Elenderson) consider it fair that a civil servant who owned a lot of property in the city should have no say in the way in which that property was taxed for municipal purposes? And, if you do not allow him to be elected to municipal office, he can have no say in the matter. The taxes he has to pay are low or high according as there are or are not qualified municipal officers. For the owner of property to have no say in the question of taxation would, I think, be unfair.

He would be in no worse position than thousands and tens of thousands of other citizens who are not elected to the municipal council. I understand that the civil servant is allowed to vote for municipal affairs. He can express an opinion in that way. I think he -would be under no hardship. Besides, the civil servant knows, when he accepts a position in the service, one condition of which is that he is to be paid out of the public treasury for his whole time, that certain privileges do not belong to him as they do to citizens who make no such engagement.

He should give his time to the service of the public, either in the shape of work or rest or recreation the better to fit him for the duties of his position.

It is easily seen that there is something to be said on both sides of this question. At the same time, so far as my experience goes-and I have had some experience in municipal affairs-I should agree with the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). With regard to gentlemen holding positions in the outside service, most of them are in the same position as those in the inside service so far as being paid for all- their time is concerned. Speaking for my own city, 1 know that the duties of an alderman or councillor require a great deal of the time of the person upon whom they devolve. A man who is not a master of his own time is not in a position to carry out the duties of alderman or councillor in that municipality at all events, so far as that municipality is concerned. I do not think the man elected for office, municipal office there, can fulfil his duty towards the government and perform his municipal duties also. Mention has been made also of the issues which arise, of the character of the issues involved in these municipal elections. While, in many cases, elections are not run on Dominion issues, yet, in almost every municipal election in this country, the influence of Dominion politics does enter to some extent; and there is no doubt that for his own welfare as well as for the general welfare of the community, I think, it is much better that the civil servant should not take any part whatever in political elections or anything of that kind. I think that is better for himself and also better for the service of the country. We recognize in our province and I presume it is so in other provinces, that an officeholder under this government is not eligible, for instance, for election to a local legislature. A civil servant who has once accepted such an office is under no greater disadvantage with regard to matter's of that kind than those who wish to run for the local legislature, A civil servant would understand that, he was debarred from seeking municipal preferment and I see no hardship in that. I believe it would be much better if this government made a hard and fast rule that persons accepting positions in the civil service of Canada were thereby debarred from entering into contests for municipal offices. A municipal council might have to do business with these civil servants on behalf of the government and if they were members of the city council the government might have an influence over them that would not be in the interest of the municipality. I endorse the opinion expressed by the Prime Minister that it would be better to make a Tule debarring officials of the Dominion 711
government from taking part in municipal politics, although I can understand that a municipality might thus be deprived of the services of very useful men.

It may be rather difficult to define where the line, if there is to be one, should be drawn. I would be inclined to accept the line laid dewn by tire Prime Minister, that is a line between those offices which command the entire time and service of the officers and those of a paltry or petty nature, which are merely adjuncts to the chief means of livelihood of the person holding them. Take the office to which I have called attention. That man has been in the service of the government for 30 years. For 26 years he enjoyed a salary of 17c a day or $60 a year. About four years ago. some change was made in the Department of Customs, under which his salary has been advanced, I think to $150. It does not seem reasonable that a man holding a position like that, purely for the convenience of the country just as many postmasters throughout Canada, hold their offices, should be debarred from becoming a member of a municipal council. After all the main consideration is to make some clear and definite rule, to make all the employees of the government understand what that rule is, and then to carry it out uniformly all over the country. That does not now seem to be done and it is for that reason that I brought this matter to the attention of the House.
Motion agreed to.

For a copy of all correspondence between the government or any member thereof, or any official of the Department of Finance, and any person or association, with reference to the conduct and affairs of the Farmers' Bank since the date of its organization.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution and the two that follow It, my desire is to get all the information possible in the hands of the government, which will enable the House and the country to form a correct opinion as to what, if any, responsibilities lie at the door of an imperfect Act on the one hand, or of an imperfect administration of the Act on the other and to define as sharply as possible, the line between the two.
The story of the history and failure of the Farmers' Bank, is, to say the least of it, not pleasant reading for the citizens of our country and no pleasant comment upon the Banking Act of which we have been so proud, and which probably w% have been prone to eulogize a little too highly. Just as I would deprecate the too great eulogy of

the Bank *Aet and the system that is founded upon it, so I would deprecate going to the other side of the scale and in a moment certainly of a good deal of stress and anxiety, where criticism is easily and largely evoked, undertaking over drastic legislation, because of any one failure or because of the circumstances which bring some of these matters more distinctly into the public mind. I do not imagine that this House proposes to lose its calmness or good temper or good sense, but at the same time the circumstances surrounding the failure of the Farmers' Bank and the public opinion which has been aroused because of that lay a duty upon this House of examining very carefully as to where the weaknesses have been and after examination of remedying them fully,, completely and, I believe, just as soon as legislation can be passed.
Now What are the circumstances of the case ? We have already had within the last few years, too few years, several rather bad bank failures. They came, some of them, suddenly; ithey struck very heavily, but there were certain circumstances in connection with them, which enabled the public to more quickly forget them. The principal circumstance was that, by the interposition of the other banks, no one lost anything. The note holders, of course, were paid and the depositors were paid, and if any loss occurred it was the loss of the capital by those who subscribed to a business venture with all the risks which surround a business venture. This is a different case. In the first place, this is a farmers' bank. The very name of it, and the canvass which was put on for stock appealed to the farming community, and it bad the effect of introducing, amongst the shareholders of the bank, a. large amount of the capital of farmers, which at the best, is earned slowly, and which when it is to be parted with in the way of loss, is a more serious matter possibly than it is to the average business man and to the business community. On that bank, being a farmers' bank, farmers were placed as directors and, without at this present time canvassing that subject at all, it certainly, in the results which have taken place, cannot be. said to have eventuated in the very best conduct of banking affairs. Fortunately, under the banking system that we have, the note holder has been in this, as in all the other cases, absolutely protected. Unless there was an avalanche of failure, a cataclysm, that would hold good under our legislation, and to my mind is a very excellent point in our banking system. When they came to invest their money in it and expected to make a profit by it, you find that they lost, not only the money they put in, but all their prospective profit as well, and have to double up by adding to Mr. FOSTER.
the amount they lost, an equal amount because under the liability clause they, have to pay the losses that have occurred. Depositors who thought that when they were depositing in the bank, it was as safe as a bank, as the rule runs, and that they would have there not only their savings, but the interest thereon, find that they are liable not perhaps to lose everything, but yet a large part of the money which they had deposited and the interest which they had hoped to gain. But what makes it more particularly hard and hitter is, that, being a farmers' bank, the farmers - putting their money into the stock of the bank, and followed up their confidence and optimism, by putting in then- earnings and savings also, as deposits hoping to strengthen the bank while at the same time, they made their own profits.
You have the institution running four years, and in that time making a banking loss of $780,000, more or less. You find it at the end of that time on the rocks, and, from the curator's reports and the examinations which have been made in the court, you find that during that four years a strange series of banking operations was taking place-directors who did not direct, inspectors who did not inspect, a Banking Act framed for the purpose of preventing abuses which did not prevent a single abuse, and a government charged with the supervision and the working of the Banking Act during the whole time not supervising, at least, not to the extent of changing by a single inch the course which was being pursued, or saving by a single dollar the money which was at stake. Now, that is the presentation of the case, that is the way it stands.
But you find more than that. The Act was supposed to set out clearly and definitely the conditions to be fulfilled before an engine of that kind could get running rights on the broad track of finance and trade in this country. You find that every provision and particular of the preliminary conditions laid down in the Bank Act have been absolutely broken, flatly defied, and yet there seemed to be no trouble at all in the bank getting in a position to do business.
Will the hon. gentleman go a little more into detail and say what provisions were not complied with?
The hon. gentleman will have all the detail before I get through if he will curb, his impatience for a moment.
That is all I want.

This is about the condition of things as it appeared. I do not want to enter into this matter too much in detail, as I am simply asking for papers, but one point that I want to bring before

the House is this: On that condition of things there is a broad feeling of unrest, and, I might say, indignation, particularly in those parts of the country where the matter comes home to the depositor on the one hand, or to the shareholder on the other, and the demand is made, if I understand, not only for an investigation, but for a remedy as well. It is on that line that I want to call the attention of the House for a few moments to the conditions laid down by the Act, and to discuss the question as to whether or not. the Act is all to blame, or the government, which called the engine into operation, is all to blame, or whether the Ac.t is partly to blame, and the supervising authority partly to blame and to apportion, as I think we must before we can come to any definite and proper conclusion, just the amount of defect that there may be in each of these and where it chiefly lies. If the Act is defective, then the supervising authority is without fault, because it had not the powers under which it could act. If the Act is not defective and still that condition of things happens that I have spoken of, then it must be that the supervising authority has been careless, or lax, or inefficient in its work. Now, then, what is the power that the Act gives? Who is responsible for the formation of a bank? There is, first, the legislative authority granting the incorporation of the bank. This parliament is responsible for the instrument calling into existence a banking company in this country. The government lays down the conditions which govern the formation and running of a bank. It then puts into the hands of certain officials and certain departments the duty of seeing that the conditions are carried out. If the conditions are ineffective the suoervising authority, as I said, has not the machinery with which to do the work, and you cannot hold it responsible, but, if the Act, in its provisions, gives a plentitude of power, then we must inquire if the supervising authority has done its duty under the powers that the Act has given. It is the company's incorporation that this House is responsible for. But the Act of incorporation cannot call the bank into existence, cannot authorize one single bit of the work to be done, cannot put a single operation into running order.
It makes the frame work, but something else has to be done to put the machine into active working order. The motive power is not the act of incorporation, it is gathered up by tire provisional directors. The provisional directors, after parliament has done its duty, under the authority of that legislation open the stock books and take subscriptions. That takes a certain amount of time and has to be done under certain regulations, and when it is all done you yet have absolutely no bank because not a stroke of business can be done up to that
point. After- the provisional directors have done their duty and have assembled the motive power, to wit, the money which is to be put into the operation, and have called the subscribers together, the duties of the provisional directors cease and the subscribers take up the work and they elect their directors, and those directors make an application for what? For running orders; for leave to go ahead. And until these running orders are given you cannot have any harm done. Then we come right to the point: Who gives the running orders? It is the government of the country through the Department of Finance. The conditions laid down are in brief these: That there shall be at least $500,000 bona fide subscribed. That word 'bona fide' is in. It. must be an actual subscription not a fake subscription. That must be subscribed in order that there shall be a backing to the bank in its operations. Is that a casual provision? No. It is elementary, it is fundamental, it is the essence of the contract arrived at by the wisdom of parliament. It was not always so, but after years of experience and much deliberation it is a fundamental condition now that if a bank shall go into operation it shall have at least $500,000 bona fide subscribed. But that is not all. It must have $250,000 of that $500,000 which is bona fide subscribed, collected in cash and put into the hands of the Minister of Finance. Both those things are fundamental and no running orders can be given until both those things are done. Now, if it is fundamental that $500,000 should be subscribed bona fide and that of that $500,000 $250,000 shall be paid up and paid into the Finance Minister, the next question comes :	Who
is to judge as to whether that $500,000 is a bona fide subscription or not; who is to be the judge as to whether that $250,000 has been paid up and is paid in? The judge is the government in and through the operation of the treasury board. Then, Sir, if anybody is made a judge as to whether these two provisions have been carried out, it is no perfunctory office that that person has to fill; it is vital. The interests not only of the shareholders but of all possible depositors, and to a large extent the business of the country are in the hands of that organization which decides whether these two actions are bona fide and whether they have been complied with. There is no prima facie complying with them, no 'possibly' complying with them, no complying with them by this or that man saying they have been complied with; no. Too big interests hang on that, too much is at stake; that must be an actual satisfactory decision come to on facts and the facts must be considered sufficient to make it beyond cavil. Is the act lame in tying the hands of the Treasury Board at that particular

point? I do not think so; I do not think the act is to blame, for what does it say:-
No certificate shall be given by the Treasury board until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the board, &c.
If these words 'to the satisfaction of the board' were not in, there might be some reasons why it might be urged that the Act was defective:-But it matters not if one man makes a solemn affidavit or ten men make a solemn affidavit, or 5,000 men make a solemn affidavit the Treasury Board is not bound to take that as evidence. It has to be satisfied ; it can call for, and it has the right, and I think the duty to call for evidence which absolutely satisfies it. I think the language of the Act is clear enough and wide enough and inclusive enough to put the responsibility upon the deciding power. Now, Sir, what happened? It turns out that in the first place $500,000 was not bona fide subscribed. In the second place it turns out that $250,000 was not bona fide paid in ; was not paid in at all. What does the curator say? He says that $170,000 was all that remained of the collections from the subscribers. More than that was collected from the subscribers, but $41,000 was paid out by and to the provisional directors for the purposes for which it was paid which are not given in detail-we will say the expenses of promotion, and the like of that. And when that $41,000 was taken out there was 'but $170,000 left of the money that actually was paid in, the whole amount paid in being $211,000. But there were notes given where cash was not paid and these notes were used, possibly. as collaterals, I do not know. But to make a long story short, there being a deficit some man borrowed $80,000, and out of his borrowings made up the sum of $250,000, and that $250,000 was deposited to the credit of the Receiver-General in the Bank of Montreal in the city of Toronto. There is actually the state of the case: The Treasury Board had the application before it. The fundamental conditions are, the subscription of $500,000, and the paying up and paying in of $250,000 of actual cash. Neither the one nor the other was done, and tlhe only way that the $250,000 came to be paid in at last was that some men, the bank not being in existence, not having running power, borrowed a sum of money and added to it. If you contend that a man can borrow $80,000 to make up the deposit, you could just as well contend that not one dollar of the $250,000 need be paid up, but that the whole of it might be borrowed, and that would satisfy the meaning of the Act. Will any man say that it would satisfy the meaning of the Act? No, nor can he say. that the borrowing of $80,000 satisfies the meaning of the Act? Yet, Mr. FOSTER.
that being the condition of. things, the Treasury Board issued the certificate on the 30th of November, 1906.
Now, I am not going to say that the case is complete, or that this House of the country should judge it until the other side is heard. I am simply putting the tiring as it is, and asking the government for all the papers and all the knowledge in their possession, in order to get all the facts together with the version of the government. That it seems to me is eminently fair. But, I am putting this case as. strongly as I can from the point of view of the sufficiency of the power which was put into the hands of the Treasury Board, and we vrill see what the information is and hear' what the government has to say.
Now, what did the government do? The government-that is, the treasury board -evidently felt that there was some trouble in -the matter. It went to the Minister of Justice for an opinion upon the evidence that came before it as to the sufficiency of the preliminary conditions being fulfilled. What was that evidence? An affidavit by Mr. Travers; that is all, so far as the Prime Minister's answer would lead me to conclude. An affidavit was handed in by Mr. Travers, stating that the money had been subscribed bona fide, and that $250,000 had been paid in, and that it lay there in the Bank of Montreal. According to the Prime Minister's answer, no other evidence was . asked. Now, suppose that there had been no discussion of the matter, no cautions, no warnings, was the Treasury Board justified in taking the affidavit of the man interested-that and nothing more, and asking for nothing more? I say, not in a case of that kind. I say that was not the proper attitude of the Treasury Board. Even if not a breath of suspicion had reached the Treasury Board, it ought to have asked something more; it ought to have made further examination; for all the interests of depositors and shareholders in the future lay upon the shoulders of those who made that decision, a decision made under great responsibility, and the grounds of it should have been as broad and as well substantiated as possible. What did the Minister,of Justice say? He said that the affidavit 'submitted; if accepted by the Treasury Board, was sufficient for them to base the certificate upon. The Minister of Justice did not estop the Treasury Board from going behind the affidavit of Mr. Travers. He said: If you accept that -as being sufficient, I suppose-you can issue the certificate; but that did not authorize the Treasury Board to issue it, or preclude it from saying, we think under the circumstances this is not enough, and we must make a further exemination. I say that even if there was no suspicion or

hint of things not being as they ought to be, more information should have been insisted upon by the Treasury Board before setting that engine going. But were there no cautions, no warnings? We ask that question. I will not say positively that there were, but this I will say, that if there were warnings, if there were cautions, written to or whispered in the ear of any member or official of the Treasury Board that matters were not as they should be- and it was known on the streets of Toronto that they were not-and that an investigation should be made, a decision given by the Treasury Board in the face of these cautions and warnings would be a very serious matter. Were any such cautions given? Were they warned? Were they expostulated with, not once, not twice, but many times? I ask the government; we will get the answer. If they were not, that part of my argument will fall. If they were, their responsibility is undeniably greater and much more heavy. Then the order to go ahead is given, and the engine starts with its full train; and it runs for four years. But there is still the Bank Act; there is still the Finance Department; there is still the government; and just as that engine stood still on the track until the Treasury Board gave it the running orders, just so it could be pulled up at any time by the same Finance Department and ordered to report its conditions. Every month certain returns had to be made; but that is not all. and that is not the most. Those returns are scheduled, and the official mind might say, we have read over the returns and they seem to be all right; we need not go further. But there is another provision which gives additional power to the Finance Department-section 113 of the Act. I will just read that. Parliament in its legislation decided upon the questions that would be asked, arranged the schedule, tried to make it take in every important particular, so that when it came each month to the Department of Finance, that department might have grounds for criticism, for judgment. It is not supposed that the returns come to the Finance Department simply to be pigeon-holed. They are there for a purpose-to be carefully scanned, to see if possible what is the condition of the bank as revealed by those returns.
What if there be anything that does not seem to be just right to the minister? If he feels he has not what he ought to have and there is something still wrong, under section 113. ' The Minister may also call for special returns from any Bank, whenever in his judgment they are necessary to afford a full complete knowledge of its condition/ That is a power virtually untrammeled. Whenever the minister likes he may call for a return, the object being to bring about information
which will guide him in ascertaining the exact condition of the bank. Those are the words of the Act ' to afford a full and complete knowledge of its condition.' This is a broad and strong power, and one which brings its own responsibility. After going orders had been issued and the bank was in operation, what happened? Among a number of others, one thing happened, the record of which we have in a non-official way. On the 11th January, 1910, the Superintendent of State Insurance in the state of New York wrote a letter to Mr. Fielding, Finance Minister. What induced the superintendent to write that letter? It was this: A man by the name of Tevis from Kentucky, with some associates, conceived the idea of buying out a mutual beneficiary insurance society or the control of it in the state of New York. It was a society which had about $3,000,000 of assets, and was in rather a comatose condition. Tevis and his associates came to Travers and borrowed $150,000 from him to buy control of that insurance company. They bought control and then immediately turned round and sold $180,000 of securities, with $150,000 of which they were to satisfy the loan. But the state of New York said, that is a mutual insurance company and the assets belong to it, and the state superintendent of insurance got busy to get back the $150,000, a part of the proceeds of the sale of securities of that society, from its lodgement in Toronto in the Farmers' Bank. He could not get it back from manager Travers, but it was necessary that it should be got quickly before liens could be put against it. He invoked the aid of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on the 11th of January. He detailed the whole of the circumstances to that minister and he said to him: Can you help me in the matter to the extent of getting information as to just how this thing stands in the bank? What was the answer? It was: THere is no government inspection and consequently we cannot act; but if you will just apply to Travers, I thirrk you can get all the information you require. But Mr. Hotchkiss had been applying to Travers and did not get the information he wanted, so that the Finance Minister, on the 11th or 12th of January was made cognizant of that kind of transaction-a transaction which, if it had been explained to a proper kind of banker-'and no banker would make $150,000 advance upon it until it had been explained to him- would have been dismissed in shorter time and in stronger words than I would take in telling you. But that was the kind of transaction of which the Finance Department was aware on the 11th of January, 1910, and that was the answer which the department gave. But after the department thought it over, it came to the conclusion that it was somewhat grave and

made up its mind to communicate with Travers, and it so informed Mr. Hotchkiss and asked him if his letter could be used. Permission was given, and a letter was written to Travers, and in due time an answer came which was transmitted to Mr. Hotchkiss, and Mr. Hotchkiss again wrote in further explanation of the transaction and still asking the Minister of Finance for his aid as far as it could be given. In the reply of Travers to Mr. Fielding, there is this phrase:	I regret that you think this an
unusual banking transaction. Therefore, the letter of Mr. Fielding to Travers, which we have not got, but which we will get, must have contained that statement. There then is the confession by the Department of Finance that this was a peculiar banking transaction, that the department knew ail about it, so far as its salient features were concerned, and that it had felt impelled to communicate with Travers and ask for an explanation. So far so good, but from the 11th of January up to the time of the closing of the bank, though often importuned, the Finance Department does not seem to have made any progress at all in aiding the insurance commissioner on the other side of the line to get at the rights of the transaction.
Now we want an explanation. Possibly a full and complete explanation may be given. We have no right to form a judgment until an explanation is given, and for my part I do not.
What else took place? We have what is called a bakers' association. What is that banking association for, and had it any particular duties or could it have exercised any rightful influence on a transaction of this kind and on the bank which was carrying it on? We had the idea in this House that whether by the direct giving of powers to the banking association or by that still stronger power which the association of all the banks must inevitably have upon any one of them, irregularities like this could be checked and managers committing them could be called down. Did the Bankers' Association know of this transaction? I should judge that they were fully appraised of it by Mr. Hotchkiss. Did they make any representations to the Finance Minister that something should be done? That information we want to get; but there is the fact that during the whole year, the Bankers' Association did not move to obtain an efficacious adjustment of that matter. Whether that association tried its influence or not we do not know. Whether its powers allowed it to exercise an influence in a ease of that kind, I am not lawyer enough to be a judge.
But, I do have faith enough in the power of the associated banks to know that, if they had got a hustle on, they could have had an explanation and a restitution from the Farmers' Bank in a very short time.

So that in this case, we evidently found no particular * advantage from the Bankers' Association. The question comes up: If the Bankers' Association did not act, was it because they had not the poweft1 If they have not the power, is it the proper thing for this parliament to enlarge their powers, so that, if the Finance Department does not do what some of us think its duty, the associated bankers will be able to remind the recalcitrant bank that it is outstepping the bounds? Not making any assertions as to whether they should have acted-I do not know whether they have the full power to act; one thing is certain, that, by some means or other, a remedy must be found. If the Banking Act is not strong enough in the powers it gives the Finance Department and the Treasury Board, give them stronger; if the Finance Department and the Treasury Board have not done their duty, let that be known to the country. If the Bankers Association is useful for balancing such things and has not the necessary powers, and we think it would be a good body to trust with such powers, let us give them the powers that are needed. The whole matter can be brought under review. For my part, there stand out clear before me two things: one is that a bank should not be able to get into operation in this Dominion under the conditions under which this bank got into operation; and the other thing is that, in this case as in the cases that have preceded it, the-weak spot is the head office and the almost complete lack of effective inspection in the head office. Does any one mean to say that a level headed inspector, one who was at nobody's beck and call, absolutely independent of the bank he was inspecting, could have gone into the Farmers' Bank at any time in 1910 or any other year during which it has been running and not, almost in a trice, have put his finger upon the weak spot in that management? But, the inspector did not inspect, from the fact that it is almost impossible, under present conditions, for the inspector to inspect the head office. When the inspector of a bank goes out to the branch offices, he is boss there, and they know it; but when he is in the head office, he is not the boss there-the manager is the boss and the inspector knows pretty well his limits.
How that should be remedied is not for me to discuss to-night; but it is for mo, and for pther members of this House, to think about,- and it is for us to discuss without fear and without favour, with the one supreme object in view of preventing such abuses in future, thereby conserving the people's confidence in the banking institutions of this country, which is the first great thing; secondly, the people's savings in these banks, and thirdly the capital which is put in good faith into these banks by men who hope to make a

success of their venture in the banking business.
That is all I have to say on the point. ^The information I have asked for is designed to bring before the House what is absolutely necessary to my mind. And let me say just one word there: I have asked for returns over and over again; I have asked for bread and have got a little bit of a stone. That is too common in the returns brought down by the government. But this is a return that will not stand for anything like that; this is a request that calls for all the information and wants it frankly, freely, fully, no matter whom it hurts. We must have it before we can remedy the evils. And it is with that view, and with these reasons to support it, that I ask the House to pass this order.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) has, in this case, asked for information. He works himself up into a great state of indignation, making out a case before the information is handed out. I think that in this, as in so many cases, it would have been more in keeping had he first obtained the information and then made his speech. He has told us that he reserves judgment until he has the information. I am glad that in one part of his remarks he made that statement. In the beginning of his remarks he said there had been loss, and there was indignation. Notwithstanding thestatement that he would suspend judgment until the information was before him, and knowing that where there is a loss of money there is indignation and an effort to flk blame, it would seem that he was endeavouring to take advantage of that state of affairs to make a case against the government which he feared he could not make when the information came down.
I do not think that any hon. membei of this House will say that in the Banking and Commerce Committee party politics ever plays any great or serious part. I think that committee is composed in large part of business men from both sides of the House who always endeavour to do business on business principles without regard to partisanship. I was not a member of the House when the Farmers Bank obtained its charter, which was in the year 1904. But that bank did not within the year prescribed, make the required deposit of $250,000, and applied, as many other banks have done, for a renewal ol its charter. This application came up when I was a member of this House and of the Banking and Commerce Committee, in 1905. The hon. member who has spoken (Mr. Foster) has endeavoured, I think I may fairly sav, to charge grave negligence to the Finance Department. The Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) is absent from the House, but he is primarily responsible for the acts of that department. I remember very well that when the Farmers' Bank Bill asking for a renewal of their charter was before the Banking and Commerce Committee, the Minister of Finance very strongly objected to tire renewal being granted ; and I remember that in that case, as in a number of other cases since, the Banking and Commerce Committee ruled against the advice of the Minister of Finance, and the Bill was carried through the committee against his hard opposition. That is not the only time it has occurred.
Oh, oh.
Did I understand the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) to speak?	.

I have been asked how that is, because I am a member of that committee, I think the Finance Minister, when he comes, will bear me out that on every occasion in the refusal to extend the time for bank charters, at any rate beyond one year, I have stood with the Finance Minister. And, on more than one occasion, the Minister of Finance has remarked : That is one question on which we agree.

Then the hon. member for Halton affords the corroborative evidence that in many cases the Finance Minister has opposed the renewal for enlarging the time of bank charters, as he did in this case. The hon. member spoke of the shareholders of the bank. I think it is the duty of this government and of this parliament to protect, as far as possible, the rights of note holders, who are well protected, and the rights of depositors. I do not know by what process of reasoning it can be argued that the government or this parliament ought to safeguard the interests of the shareholders of a bank more than the rights of the shareholders in any other financial or other institution. The shareholders enter into the banking business, they elect their own officers, their own general manager, their own board of directors, and they have the same rights, the same privileges, the same opportunities of guarding the money that they have put into the stock of the bank that any other shareholder has. In this case the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said that there had been a neglect and an overlooking of the preliminary provisions on that point. I asked him to speak more in detail and he said he would later on. I suppose he did and that he thought he was giving me the information for which I had asked when he said that the Bank Act points out that there must be $500,000 in stock, in bona fide subscriptions. The Act does say so. He argued further, and correctly, that the Banking Act, section 15, says:

No certificate shall be given by the treasury board until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the board, by affidavit or otherwise, that all the requirements of this Act and of the special Act of incorporation of the bank, as to the payment required to be made to the minister, the election of directors,

and so forth-
-have been complied with.
The hon. member and others will note that section 15 says:-
Until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the board, by affidavit or otherwise.
The board may, if they choose, accept the bald statement of the incorporators, or they may require an affidavit. The Act seems to imply that if an affidavit is obtained that is all the evidence they may naturally be expected to ask for or require. But the hon. gentleman says they accepted the affidavit of Travers, who is a man interested. Let me say they accepted the affidavit of Travers, who was the man of all men who knew the facts. Affidavits in support of many actions in court are taken from the men interested because they are the men who have the knowledge, perhaps the only men who have, or ought to have, the knowledge. It turns out that part of that $250,000 was borrowed money. The Fina&ce Department and the Treasury Board have given the right to many, many banks to do business; had they any greater ground in this case to suspect that part of the deposit had been borrowed than in any other case, or than they will have in any case in the future? If the hon. gentleman knows any reason now why the treasury board should have had suspicions, when that part of the $250,000 was borrowed and not paid in the usual way, he might state what information he has in that regard. It was not suspected, the Treasury Board had no such suspicion. It is all right for us now that the steed has been stolen to look back, but there w'as no reason then to suspect any wrongdoing. Mr. Travers is known now to have been a dishonest man, or a very weak man, but nobody knew that at the time. Many of the provisional directors of the bank were known to be men of good character and repute, and still they have that reputation as honest business men, so I repeat there is no reason why the Treasury Board should have had any such suspicions. The hon. gentleman has said: If there were hints and warnings. That is a style and argument characteristic of him: If there were rumours, if there were hints, if there were warnings-then he immediately goes on to build up his case as if he had proven there were hints and warnings, although he has not afforded one tittle of proof that there was anything of the kind. If I say that actually there were no hints or warnings the hon. gentleman cannot con-Mr. MILLER.
tradiet me, because he does not know and he has no information that there were any hints or warnings, or that the Treasury Board or the Finance Department, or the minister had any reason to suspect that these people were not honestly doing an honest business.

Would not the hon. gentleman regard it as the duty of the Treasury Board to go beyond the mere statement of an interested party and ascertain from the stock books in what position they stood, if $500,000 was bona fide subscribed, if $250,000 in cash was bona fide paid in on the spot, because I assume the books would show it unless they are falsified? Would he not regard it as the duty of the Treasury Board' to . make at least that inquiry?

I would ask the hon. gentleman whether any person in the whole history of the government of Canada has ever made any such hint or whether any person on either side of the House when the Bank Act was being framed, or at its last or any former revision, has ever hinted that an affidavit as required by the Act, was not sufficient evidence ?	.
The hon. member has not answered the question.

I quite agree with the hon. member for North Toronto that if at that stage there had been any warnings or hints, or any reason for the Treasury Board to believe that these people weTe not honest and the statement in the affidavit untrue, they would have had reason to go further afield for information.
Will my hon. friend state from actual knowledge, that there were no cautions, no hints, no warnings at. that, time ?
We have often heard it said that it is not possible to proMe a negative. I am not building up a case against the government.
You do not need to say that.

If I could, I would not be unfair enough to endeavour to build up a case against the hon. member for North Toronto, upon any accusation whatever, upon fancied facts or mere Tumours, nor has the hon. member the right to endeavour to build up a case against the Finance Minister, the department or the Treasury Board, upon rumours or street gossip, and I say, it is too often his habit, and it would be to his credit, if he did not do it as often as he does in this House.
My hon. friend has stated positively that I had no such, information. On what ground does he make that statement ?
I made no such statement. I said: If I say that there was no hint, that there was no warning, the bon. member for North Toronto cannot contradict me, because he does not know.
How do you know ?

I know that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), does not know. I know it very well, because I know if he had the evidence, he would have produced it, and he did not produce it. I am not pretending to giv<j evidence for any one. The hon. gentleman is endeavouring to build up a case on evidence that he assumed to have and did not have.
The hon. member has spoken of the the Bankers' Association. The Bankers' Association are in a much better position to hear any rumours that may be heard.

I assume the. hon. gentleman is making a defence, possibly for the government, possibly for somebody else. But if the treasury board or any of its members were informed that this $250,000 was not raised in such a manner as is described by the banking Act, would he then consider that the affidavit of Mr. Travers should be accepted without any further inquiry ?

That would depend very much upon the source from which that information came, and the shape in which .it came. I can easily understand, and I do not know' whether it was the case in this instance or not, that financial companies already existing, other banks, jealous of the incorporation of a new bank, might cause a rumour to be circulated that no one might' reasonably rely upon, but if any person had absolutely that information he ought to have given it to the Treasury Board, before the certificate was issued, not as a mere rumour, but in some such shape that the Treasury Board could have accepted it, and would have had a reasonable right to believe that the information was true. I do not believe that the Treasury Board could act on mere rumour at all.
The hon. member for North Toronto spoke of the Bankers' Association. I was saying when the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) rose, that the Bankers' Association are in a much better position to know what is going on in banking circles than anybody else. The Bankers' Association are always jealous of the reputation of the banks because if one bank fails and causes loss to depositors and shareholders it always reflects upon and injures the credit of other banks as was done in this case. Therefore, the members of the association are always careful to give warning to the Finance Department in cases where the circumstances
seem to justify it, and I do not believe that any such warning ever came to the Finance Department of the Minister of Finance from the Bankers' Association. The hon. member for North Toronto has pointed out section 113 of the Bank Act which does give the Finance Department or the Minister of Finance the right to call for special returns.
The minister may also call for special returns from any bank, whenever, in his judgment, they are necessary to afford a full and complete knowledge of its conditions.
Section 147 of the Bank Act provides for regular monthly returns showing the financial condition of the bank:
Every bank which neglects to make up and send to the minister, within the first fifteen days of any month, any monthly return by this Act required to be made up and sent in within the said fifteen days, exhibiting the condition of the bank on the last juridical day of the month last preceding, and signed in the manner and by the persons by this Act required, shall incur a penalty of fifty dollars for each and every day, after the expiration of such time, during which the bank neglects to make and send in such return.
So that the Minister of Finance must have had a return less.than a month from the time he received a warning, in so far as it was a warning from the notice alleged to have been received from some one	in	the	United States
That return which showed, over the signature of the officials of the bank, the standing of the bank had been received not more than a month prior to that notice so that it was not necessary for a special return, nor could anything be gained by seeking such a special return. While this section pointed- out by the hon. member for North Toronto gives the Minister the right to call for special returns there was no section of the Banking Act that gave the Minister of Finance the right to send any official into any bank to make an inspection of its books. The Bank Act expressly says that no person shall have that right except the directors and officials of the bank. There was some gentleman in the State of New York who it is said did advise the Minister of Finance that a loan of $150,000 had been made that was irregular. What would any person expect the Minister of Finance to do in such a case? He writes to Mr. Travers, the general manager of the bank, and points out that the loan was not a regular loan, that it was not properly made. This is not the only instance, I imagine, in which the Minister of Finance has had to point out to many men, managers of banks, insurance, loan and trust companies that the business that they were doing was irregular business not being honestly-I will not say honestly-but not being regularly carried on. In most cases it would be sufficient to call

the attention of the manager, or the managing director, to the irregularity in the business that was being carried on. There was no neglect of duty. As to whether, in view of what has taken place in regard to the failure of two or three banks in the last few years, there ought to be an amendment to the Bank Act and whether the Department of Finance ought to have greater power, is another question. The Minister of Finance evidently thought, before the failure of the Farmers' Bank, not influenced in any way by that failure because the failure had not taken place at the time, that the depositors and shareholders of a bank ought to have greater protection than the Bank Act at present gives them because in section 56 of the new Bank Act submitted to this House there is provision for the election of shareholders' inspectors. This principle has been excepted by the Bank of Nova Scotia because for some time the shareholders have had the right to appoint shareholders' inspectors and inspections have been made by the shareholders' inspectors of that bank. The Minister of Finance is carrying that into the proposed new Bank Act. I do not know that I have really anything more to say as to that. I do not think it is fair at this time, simply because the Farmers' Bank has failed, to endeavour to make any capital out of any accusation against the Minister of Finance. I think that in the newspapers some very unfair accusations and charges have been made. We cannot help what is done in the newspapers, but I think that the hon. member for North Toronto is too old a parliamentarian to properly and fairly take advantage of any feeling which exists at the present time to make charees against the Minister of Finance or the Finance Department that are dependent entirely on rumour which has probably not the slightest foundation in fact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all the information in the hands of the government in respect to this matter will be brought down, in the language of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) fully, frankly and freely. There is no reason at all why all the particulars with regard to the formation of this bank and every other transaction should not be brought down absolutely as it is in the records of the government. I cannot but believe that my hon. friend from North Toronto on reflection, will agree with my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) that it would have been more advisable if he had waited until the whole of the information was before the House to make the comments which he has made, because I have reason to think that some of his surmises will not be borne out by the facts. If there has been laxness on Mr. MILLER.
the part of anybody, I think everybody in this House must bear the blame. This Farmers' Bank was incorporated-I forget in what year now. But it did not organize during the time allowed it in which to complete its organization. It had to come back to parliament, and it got an extension of time. It had to come back again to get a further extension of delay. I know, and, in fact, it has been stated by my hon. friend from South Grey, that there was some hesitancy on the part of the Committee on Banking and Commerce to allow this renewal of the charter which had been given to the Farmers' Bank. Perhaps it may be after all that this hesitation was overborne by the very title of the bank itself. It was to be a farmers' bank. It was to be outside of the general curriculum of the other banks, and if the committee had refused it incorporation it is quite probable that there would have been a great deal of murmuring and it is quite possible that it might have been said that when the farming community came to have a bank of their own the Bankers' Association were powerful enough to prevent incorporation being given. If the incorporation had been refused it is quite possible that instead of 1 aving the government blamed in the year 1910, it would have been blamed in the year 1905 because this incorporation was not granted. At all# events, whatever may have been the motive, the committee thought it advisable to give the charter, and they renewed it not once, but twice. When it came before parliament, so far as my memory serves, not a word of dissent was heard from anybody. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) passes rather lightly over these facts, but he insisted on two points as to which he thought the_ government was to blame, basing his opinion on the information which he has before him at the present moment. The first of these was as to the action of the Treasury Board in giving a certificate to the bank, and the second with reference to a certain transaction w'hicli was mentioned in the press only a few days ago. With regard to the certificate granted by the Treasury Board, in considering the information we have before us at present, can any one say that the Treasury Board wuts in any way blam-able. It may be said that other facts will be disclosed, although I do not think so, but even if the insinuation made by my hon. friend (Mr, Foster) turned out to be true, namely, that there had been outside information given to the Minister of Finance; or to some one I do not know who, would it have been advisable on the part of the board to exercise even more than the caution they did? Under our present information, I ask any man in this House, does he believe that the Treasury Board which is presided over by the Minister of

Finance was in any way blamable in granting the certificate? The evidence before the Treasury Board upon which the certificate was issued that the bank should commence operations, was the very substantial fact that the $250,000 required by law was deposited to the credit of the Receiver General. This was accompanied by an affidavit that all the formalties had been complied with and that all the necessary requirements enacted by law had been carefully observed. Could any man under these circumstances have his imagination so perverted as to suppose that there was something wrong behind this? I ask any business man in this chamber, if, under such circumstances he would not have acted just as the Minister of Finance did, namely, take the advice of the Minister of Justice as to whether the law had been complied with, and then give a certificate. I am not a member of the Treasury Board, and I do not know what tome place, but on the evidence before us at present I do not think any one will attach blame to the Minister of Finance. Then we come to the second point made by my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) with reference to the particular transaction revealed but a few days ago by the correspondence published in the press as having taken place between Mr. Hotchkiss, superintendent of insurance for New York state, and the Minister of Finance.

May I be permitted to put the same question that I put to the hon. member for South Grey? Would not the right hon. gentleman think it the duty of the Treasury Board, having this information from disinterested parties, to try in some way to verify the allegations by an examination of the books of the bank? That would be the best way to ascertain whether the stock had been subscribed bona fide and whether the amount the law required had been paid up bona fide.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think so. I should think that the proper man to give an affidavit was Mr. Travers, manager oi the bank. It has been stated by the hon. member for North Toronto that the affidavit which had been put in the hands of the government was false. That mav be, but my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) knows as well as I do that there never was a law passed by the legislature of any country which was not violated at some time or other. You can pass all the laws you want to in this parliament, or any other, 'but so long as human nature is what it is there will, unfortunately, be some one found to violate that law. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) states that the affidavit put in the hands of the Minister of Finance was false, but I put it to any business man if he would be likely to suppose, in a similar transaction, that such was the ease. Now,
the second point raised by my hon. friend was with regard to the correspondence between Mr. Hotchkiss and the Minister of Finance. It may be that the law is defective in this respect, but at all events the Minister of Finance answered very properly that we had no bank inspection provided for in our Act, and, therefore, he could not assist Mr. Hotchkiss as that gentleman wanted him to. I may observe, by way of parenthesis, that in the Bill now before the House to renew the Bank Act, the Minister of Finance has himself suggested that the law be amended, and he _ provides for _ a different audit, which, if it had been in force previously, possibly would have prevented some transactions of the Farmers' Bank. But there was no inspection provided for in our law at that time, and the Minister of Finance very properly answered that he had no authority to give Mr. Hotchkiss the information asked for, or to take the proceedings which Mr. Hotchkiss wanted him to take. But the Minister of Finance was not satisfied with that; he at once wrote to Mr. Travers, manager of the bank, informing him of the complaint which had been made against him. What followed then? If what I am informed is the fact, then the comments of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) fall to the ground. I am informed-I have not had time to verify the information-that this transaction between the Farmers' Bank and Mr. Tevis for the purchase of the assets of this Mutual Insurance Company fell through and was not carried out, and that the securities which Mr. Hotchkiss was pfter were returned to him. If that be so the Minister of Finance had nothing more to do when he was informed that the transaction about which complaint was made had been called off for some reason or other, and the Minister of Finance would be free from the blame which the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) tries to place upon him. The Bankers' Association is also free from the -blame he tries to place upon it, because he said-if I have taken his words correctly-that from the Ilth of January up to the present time, no explanation has been given of this transaction. Well, no explanation has been given of the transaction, because, if I am correctly informed, the transaction was never completed, and the moment it fell through there was nothing more to inquire about it. I think, therefore, that my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) was a little premature in his judgment.
I do nqt think I was premature, and if my right hon. Mend will allow me to say it, I do not think his information covers all the ground.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know whether it does or not, but at all events it would be better for me and for the hon. gentleman to reserve our observations until

we know all the particulars. However, if my information be correct, I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that his opinions are a little premature.

There is just one observation which I would like to make with regard to the duty of the Treasury Board in such cases. I do not propose to pass any judgment upon the transaction, nor do I understand that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has done so, in the absence of the evidence that is to be brought down, and before the inquiry that possibly may have been made. But I would like to point out to the Prime Minister, and to the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) that the provisions of section 15 seem to go a little further than the Prime Minister has intimated. The provisions of section 15 are:
No certificate shall be given by the Treasury Board until it has been shown to the satisfaction of the board, by affidavit or otherwise, that all the requirements of this Act and the special Act of incorporation of the bank have been complied with.
The expression, * by affidavit or otherwise ' is merely directory as to the character of the evidence which may or may not be accepted. The definite and specific provision of section 15 is that the Treasury Board must be satisfied. It is the right of the Treasury Board-more than that, it is the duty of the Treasury Board-to withhold that certificate until it is fully satisfied.

Does the hon. gentleman think there was anything in this case that was unusual at that time, that ought to have made the Treasury Board act otherwise with this bank than they had been in the habit of acting with others?

My hon. friend told us a moment ago that none of us could know anything about it, and therefore, from his own standpoint, his question is meaningless. I have no personal knowledge of what took place at that time; he reminded us that none of us could have any personal knowledge; therefore, his question is irrelevant at the present moment. I am pointing out to the Prime Minister that whether an affidavit was made or not is not the question. The question is whether or . not the Treasury Board was satisfied, whether or not under the circumstances it had a right to report itself as satisfied. As my Iron, friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, it is not a light matter to give a bank in this country the power to begin business. The statute has very properly required that certain very distinct and definite conditions shall be" complied with, and the last condition of all is that the Treasury Board, as trustees for the whole people of Canada, shall be absolutely satisfied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Treasury Board in this case was satisfied with the deposit of the money and the affidavit.

As it turns out, they were entirely wrong in being so satisfied, if my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is right in his statement of what has transpired in connection with the liquidation of the bank. The Treasury Board were satisfied, but they ought not to have been satisfied, because the actual conditions, not the conditions as stated in the affidavit, should not have permitted that bank to receive a certificate from the Treasury Board. The Prime Minister argued that Mr. Travers was the man who knew more about this than any one else, and therefore when he made a certain affidavit, the Treasury Board, without any further inquiry, without calling for the production of the stock books, without making an investigation which they might have made, should grant a certificate as a matter of course. If that is what the Prime Minister intended to convey to the House, I do_ not agree with him. I say that, pre-eminently in a case where the man making the affidavit is the man who, to the knowledge of every one in the country, was the promoter of the bank, it would have been a very proper and a very reasonable thing, and not a very unusual thing, for the Treasury Board to say, we have your declaration as to all these matters, but we desire to make further inquiries and to have the production of certain other documents and papers. It is quite apparent to us now that if the government had taken that reasonable and not very unusual course, the condition of affairs would not now be so lamentably against the interest of many people in this country as it is, if we can judge by the press reports, in the case of this bank. However, I do not desire to pass judgment on the action of the government in that regard until we have the papers and until we have possibly some further inquiry into the whole matter.
Motion agreed to.

For a copy of the full report and finding of the curator of the Farmers' Bank, up to the time of his appointment as liquidator of the same by the shareholders for the requisition of which authority is given to the Minister of Finance by section 122 of the Bank Act.
He said:	I suppose the Finance Department has already called for that and has it in its possession; but if it has not, the minister has the right to call for it. A curator's report is as full a resume of the whole situation as we can get without a minute legal investigation, and would be very satisfactory for us to have.
Motion agreed to.
For a copy of the by-laws, rules and regulations of the Canadian Bankers' Association as approved by the Treasury Board and now in effect.
Motion agreed to.
Bill (No. 15) to amend the Canada Medical Act-Mr. Black-read the second time.

That it be referred to a special committee composed of Messrs. Black, Daniel, Beland, Paquet, Schaffner, Roche, Neeley, Currie (Prince Edward), Chisholm (Huron), Sproule, Cash, Chisholm (Inverness), McAllister, Rankin and Carvell.
He said: I do not anticipate any opposition to this Bill at all. These amendments have been submitted to the medical councils and associations of every province and have been approved by them all. These associations and councils represent between 6,000 and 7,000 medical men in the Dominion. When this Bill was introduced in 1902, it met with a good deal of opposition, but all that opposition has passed away and from Vancouver to Halifax, as far as the medical profession is concerned, they are in favour of it.
Motion agreed to.
Sir Wilfrid LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
I would like to say to the Prime Minister that the report we were speaking about a little while ago, was the one of 1902. I would ask that he take note of this and see that we get it.

Order (No. 6) was asked to stand at the request of the right hon. the Prime Minister on his assertion doubtless made innocently though wrongly, that I was out of the House. It was my desire that this order should be gone on with. It was left to stand until the next private members' day, and I should iike to know what disposition is proposed to be made of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These orders were called at a quarter before midnight, so that this Bill could not be disposed of at the present sitting. We have reached the hour of adjournment and there was no discourtesy intended to my hon. friend in not going on with his measure. There are as many on this side who wish to discuss it, as on the other, and no doubt on Monday next we can reach it.

When I gave notice.of my intention to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a certain motion, I was under the impression from what I had seen in the newspapers that the Finance Minister would be in his place to-morrow, I have since learned that he will not, and therefore announce my intention to bring on the motion at the earliest possible opportunity after his return.
If convenient, my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), would like to bring on to-morrow, a motion with regard to the amounts paid in Ottawa for the use of rented buildings.
What buildings ?
We will send my hon. friend a copy of the motion some time tomorrow forenoon.
I shall be very glad if you will do so.
What business to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I intend to take up some Bills, but if convenient will take up Supply the first order to-morrow- Public Works.
